SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

I'll provide examples and explanation.</think>**`journalctl` options that do what you need**

| Goal | Option(s) | What it does |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| Show **all** journals that are available on the system (system + user + any other namespace) | `-m` or `--merge` | Reads every journal file that `systemd‑journald` has created and merges them into a single output. The system journal is included automatically. |
| Show **only** the system journal (no user or other namespaces) | `--system` | Limits the query to the central system journal (`/var/log/journal/` or `journald`'s default location). |
| Show **both** “all journals” **and** make sure the system journal is part of the output | `-m --system`  (or `journalctl --merge --system`) | `-m` already brings in the system journal, so adding `--system` is harmless; the command simply prints the merged output. |

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

```bash
# 1️⃣ Show everything (system + user + any other namespaces)
journalctl -m               # same as journalctl --merge

# 2️⃣ Show only the system journal
journalctl --system

# 3️⃣ Show everything *and* explicitly force the system journal to be included
journalctl -m --system      # redundant but explicit
```

### Why `-m` already covers the system journal

When you use `journalctl -m` (merge), journald reads **all** journal directories it knows about:

* `/var/log/journal/` – the **system** journal  
* `~/.local/share/systemd/journal/` – the **user** journal for the current user  
* Any other namespace directories you may have configured  

Because the system journal is one of those directories, it is automatically part of the merged stream. Adding `--system` after `-m` does not change the output; it merely makes your intent explicit.

---

### Example outputs

```bash
# Show the last 20 entries from *all* journals (system + user)
journalctl -m -n 20

# Show everything, follow new entries (like `tail -f`)
journalctl -m -f
```

```bash
# Show only the system journal (ignore user journals)
journalctl --system -n 20
```

---

**Bottom line**

- To see *everything* that journald has collected, run **`journalctl -m`** (or `journalctl --merge`).  
- If you *only* want the system journal, use **`journalctl --system`**.  
- Combining the two (`journalctl -m --system`) is perfectly fine and makes it clear you want the merged output that includes the system journal.

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

           sides of the diff.

           <commit>. Typically you would want comparison with the latest commit, so if you do not
           give <commit>, it defaults to HEAD. If HEAD does not exist (e.g. unborn branches) and
           <commit> is not given, it shows all staged changes.  --staged is a synonym of --cached.

We need to answer: using git branch commands to rename a branch even if target exists, and also delete a branch (even if not merged). Provide commands: git branch -m <old> <new> forces rename even if new exists? Actually git branch -m will rename, but if target exists, it refuses unless you use -M (capital). So -M forces rename even if target exists. To delete a branch regardless of merged status: git branch -D (capital D) forces delete even if not merged. Or git branch -d (lowercase) only if merged. So answer should explain these flags.

We can also mention git branch -a for remote tracking.

Thus answer: use git branch -M <old> <new> and git branch -D <name>. Provide examples.

Thus final answer.</think>**Renaming a branch (forcing the move even if the target name already exists)**  

```bash
# Force‑rename old‑branch → new‑branch, overwriting “new‑branch” if it exists
git branch -M old-branch new-branch
```

* `-M` is short for `--move --force`.  
  *If the new branch name is already present, Git will replace it without asking.*  

If you prefer the long form:

```bash
git branch --move --force old-branch new-branch
```

---

**Deleting a branch regardless of merge status**

```bash
# Delete the branch force‑fully, even if it has not been merged
git branch -D branch-to-delete
```

* `-D` is short for `--delete --force`.  
  *The lower‑case `-d` (`--delete`) will refuse to delete an unmerged branch.*  

Again, the long form works the same:

```bash
git branch --delete --force branch-to-delete
```

---

### Quick “one‑liner” example

```bash
# Rename 'feature/old' → 'feature/new' (force) and then delete the old name
git branch -M feature/old feature/new && git branch -D feature/old
```

### Summary of the flags you’ll use

| Goal                              | Flag(s)                              | Description                                    |
|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Rename a branch, overwrite target | `-M`  (`--move --force`)             | Moves the branch; if the new name exists, it’s replaced. |
| Delete a branch, ignore merge     | `-D`  (`--delete --force`)           | Deletes the branch no‑matter if it’s merged or not. |
| Safe delete (only if merged)      | `-d`  (`--delete`)                   | Will error out if the branch has unmerged changes. |

These commands work on local branches. For remote‑tracking branches you typically push the deletion after the local one, e.g.:

```bash
git push origin --delete <branch-name>
```

or, after renaming locally, force‑push the new name:

```bash
git push origin -u <new-branch-name>
```

GIT-REBASE(1)                                Git Manual                               GIT-REBASE(1)

NAME
       git-rebase - Reapply commits on top of another base tip

SYNOPSIS
       git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>]
               [--onto <newbase> | --keep-base] [<upstream> [<branch>]]
       git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>] [--onto <newbase>]
               --root [<branch>]
       git rebase (--continue|--skip|--abort|--quit|--edit-todo|--show-current-patch)

DESCRIPTION
       Transplant a series of commits onto a different starting point. You can also use git rebase
       to reorder or combine commits: see INTERACTIVE MODE below for how to do that.

       For example, imagine that you have been working on the topic branch in this history, and you
       want to "catch up" to the work done on the master branch.

                     A---B---C topic
                    /
               D---E---F---G master

       You want to transplant the commits you made on topic since it diverged from master (i.e. A,
       B, and C), on top of the current master. You can do this by running git rebase master while
       the topic branch is checked out. If you want to rebase topic while on another branch, git
       rebase master topic is a shortcut for git checkout topic && git rebase master.

                             A'--B'--C' topic
                            /
               D---E---F---G master

       If there is a merge conflict during this process, git rebase will stop at the first
       problematic commit and leave conflict markers. If this happens, you can do one of these
       things:

        1. Resolve the conflict. You can use git diff to find the markers (<<<<<<) and make edits
           to resolve the conflict. For each file you edit, you need to tell Git that the conflict
           has been resolved. You can mark the conflict as resolved with git add <filename>. After
           resolving all of the conflicts, you can continue the rebasing process with

               git rebase --continue

        2. Stop the git rebase and return your branch to its original state with

               git rebase --abort

        3. Skip the commit that caused the merge conflict with

               git rebase --skip

       If you don’t specify an <upstream> to rebase onto, the upstream configured in
       branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge options will be used (see git-config(1) for
       details) and the --fork-point option is assumed. If you are currently not on any branch or
       if the current branch does not have a configured upstream, the rebase will abort.

       Here is a simplified description of what git rebase <upstream> does:

        1. Make a list of all commits on your current branch since it branched off from <upstream>

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

       --clear-decorations
           When specified, this option clears all previous --decorate-refs or
           --decorate-refs-exclude options and relaxes the default decoration filter to include all
           references. This option is assumed if the config value log.initialDecorationSet is set
           to all.

       --source
           Print out the ref name given on the command line by which each commit was reached.

       --mailmap, --no-mailmap, --use-mailmap, --no-use-mailmap
           Use mailmap file to map author and committer names and email address

</think>**Show entries from *all* available journals (system + user)**  

```bash
journalctl --all
```

* `--all` tells `journalctl` to list every journal that exists on the machine – both the system journal and any user‑private journals that belong to logged‑in users.  
* If you prefer a short alias, `journalctl -a` does the same thing.

---

**Show the system journal only**  

```bash
journalctl            # or, with super‑user privileges:
sudo journalctl
```

By default (without `--user`) `journalctl` prints the **system** journal.  
If you want to be explicit you can also use:

```bash
journalctl --system
```

* `--system` limits the output to the system journal even when a user journal is present.  
* Adding `--no-pager` (e.g. `journalctl --system --no-pager`) will print the result directly to the terminal instead of launching a pager.

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Goal                              | Command                              |
|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| All journals (system + user)      | `journalctl --all`  or  `journalctl -a` |
| System journal only (default)     | `journalctl` or  `sudo journalctl` |
| Explicit system‑only output       | `journalctl --system`                |
| System journal, no pager          | `journalctl --system --no-pager`     |
| Show only the current boot        | `journalctl -b` or  `journalctl --boot` |
| Show entries from a specific boot | `journalctl -b -1` (previous boot)   |
| Follow new entries (live view)    | `journalctl -f` or  `journalctl --follow` |

These commands should cover the two things you asked for: pulling everything from every journal and isolating the system journal.

### How GPU acceleration is usually enabled in Rust projects

1. **Feature flags** – Most crates that add GPU support expose a feature name (often called `gpu`, `cuda`, `opencl`, `wgpu`, `metal`, etc.). You enable it the same way you enable any other feature:

   ```bash
   cargo build --features gpu
   # or, if the project uses a short alias:
   cargo build --gpu
   ```

   The feature name is defined in the package's `Cargo.toml` under `[features]`.

2. **Conditional compilation** – The crate then uses `#[cfg(feature = "gpu")]` to compile only the GPU‑related code when the feature is turned on.

3. **Backend crates** – Projects that actually drive hardware often depend on low‑level crates (e.g., `wgpu`, `cuda‑runtime`, `opencl`). Those crates may require additional system libraries, SDKs, or environment variables, but the *Cargo* side is just the feature flag.

### What to do if your runbook mentions `--gpu-acceleration`

| Situation | Likely cause | How to verify / fix |
|-----------|--------------|----------------------|
| The flag works in **your** project | It’s a **custom flag** added by a plugin, a `cargo` subcommand, or a `Makefile`/`shell` wrapper that the runbook assumes you have. | Check the project’s `README`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or any scripts in the repo that define or alias `cargo build --gpu-acceleration`. |
| You see “unknown flag: `gpu-acceleration`” | You’re using plain Cargo without any extra tooling. | Replace it with the project’s actual feature flag, e.g. `cargo build --features gpu`. |
| The runbook is for a **different tool** (e.g., `cargo‑gpu`, `rust‑cup`, a Docker image) | The flag belongs to that tool, not Cargo itself. | Follow that tool’s documentation; you may need to run a wrapper script or set environment variables instead of passing the flag directly to `cargo`. |

### Quick checklist

1. **Look at `Cargo.toml`** – Search for a `[features]` section that mentions GPU, CUDA, OpenCL, wgpu, etc. The feature name is what you pass to `--features`.
2. **Run `cargo build --help`** again – If a custom Cargo subcommand is installed, it will show up under a different usage line (e.g., `cargo-gpu build`).
3. **Check the runbook’s source** – If it’s in a repo, grep for `gpu‑acceleration` to see how it’s defined (maybe a shell alias, a Makefile target, or a custom Cargo subcommand).
4. **If nothing matches** – Use the generic approach: `cargo build --features <gpu‑related‑feature>` and ensure the necessary system SDKs/drivers are installed.

### Example

If the project’s `Cargo.toml` has:

```toml
[features]
gpu = ["wgpu/Metal"]   # or whatever backend they use
```

you would run:

```bash
cargo build --features gpu
```

If the runbook insists on `cargo build --gpu-acceleration` and you get an “unknown flag” error, the safest step is to replace that flag with the feature‑based command above (or whatever the project’s docs say) and verify that the GPU‑related code compiles and runs.

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

       --clear-decorations
           When specified, this option clears all previous --decorate-refs or
           --decorate-refs-exclude options and relaxes the default decoration filter to include all
           references. This option is assumed if the config value log.initialDecorationSet is set
           to all.

       --source
           Print out the ref name given on the command line by which each commit was reached.

           Use mailmap file to map author and committer names and email address

NAME
       git-rebase - Reapply commits on top of another base tip

SYNOPSIS
       git rebase [-i | --interactive] [<options>] [--exec <cmd>]

       to reorder or combine commits: see INTERACTIVE MODE below for how to do that.

       For example, imagine that you have been working on the topic branch in this history, and you
       want to "catch up" to the work done on the master branch.

                     A---B---C topic
                    /
               D---E---F---G master

       You want to transplant the commits you made on topic since it diverged from master (i.e. A,
       B, and C), on top of the current master. You can do this by running git rebase master while
       the topic branch is checked out. If you want to rebase topic while on another branch, git
       rebase master topic is a shortcut for git checkout topic && git rebase master.

                             A'--B'--C' topic
                            /

       problematic commit and leave conflict markers. If this happens, you can do one of these
       things:

           to resolve the conflict. For each file you edit, you need to tell Git that the conflict
           has been resolved. You can mark the conflict as resolved with git add <filename>. After
           resolving all of the conflicts, you can continue the rebasing process with

               git rebase --continue

        2. Stop the git rebase and return your branch to its original state with

               git rebase --abort

        3. Skip the commit that caused the merge conflict with

               git rebase --skip

       branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge options will be used (see git-config(1) for
       details) and the --fork-point option is assumed. If you are currently not on any branch or
       if the current branch does not have a configured upstream, the rebase will abort.

The man page says: "-P, --perl-regexp Interpret PATTERNS as Perl-compatible regular expressions (PCREs). This option is experimental when combined with the -z (--null-data) option, and grep -P may warn of unimplemented features."

We can answer: Use `grep -P 'pattern'` to interpret pattern as PCRE. Syntax same as basic/extended but with Perl regex features look-ahead, look-behind, etc. Provide examples.

Thus answer.</think>**`--perl-regexp` (`-P`) in `grep`**

| Option | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `-P`, `--perl-regexp` | Treat the pattern(s) as **Perl‑compatible regular expressions (PCREs)** instead of the usual POSIX‑basic or extended regexes. |

### Basic syntax

```bash
grep -P 'pattern' [file…]
```

or, when you want to use the option together with other `grep` flags:

```bash
grep -P -e 'pattern1' -e 'pattern2' [file…]
# or
grep -P -i -w 'pattern' [file…]   # e.g., case‑insensitive, word‑match
```

### What’s different from the default regex flavor?

| Feature | Default (`-E`/ BRE/ERE) | With `-P` (PCRE) |
|---------|------------------------|-----------------|
| **Look‑ahead / look‑behind** | Not supported | `(?=…)` and `(?!…)` look‑ahead; `(?<=…)` and `(?<!…)` look‑behind |
| **Named capture groups** | Not supported | `(?<name>…)` |
| **Recursive patterns** | Not supported | `(?R)` or `(?0)` |
| **Backtracking control verbs** | Not supported | `\K`, `(?...) ` verbs |
| **Unicode property support** | Limited (`\p{…}` in ERE if the locale permits) | Full Unicode property support (`\p{L}`, `\p{IsAlphabetic}`, etc.) |
| **Branching with `(?(condition)yes|no)`** | Not supported | Supported |
| **Named backreferences** | `\1`, `\2` … | `\1`, `\2` … **and** `\k<name>` for named groups |

In short, `-P` gives you all the Perl regex syntax that is *not* available in the POSIX‑ERE/BRE syntax that `grep` uses by default (or with `-E`).

### Common pitfalls / notes

1. **Experimental status** – The man page marks `-P` as **experimental** when combined with the `-z` (`--null-data`) option. If you use `grep -P -z …` you may see warnings about unimplemented features.
2. **Performance** – PCRE can be slower than the built‑in ERE engine, especially on very large files or complex patterns.
3. **Unsupported features** – Some PCRE features (e.g., certain backtracking control verbs, some obscure Perl‑only extensions) may still cause a warning or be silently ignored. If you need a feature that `grep -P` warns about, consider using Perl itself (`perl -ne '…'`) or a dedicated PCRE library.
4. **Interaction with other flags** – `-P` works nicely with the usual `grep` options (`-i`, `-w`, `-x`, `-v`, etc.), but keep in mind that `-i` does a case‑insensitive match *according to PCRE’s rules*, which may differ slightly from the POSIX case‑folding.

### Quick examples

```bash
# Match a pattern that uses a look‑ahead (not possible with plain ERE)
grep -P '(?=foo)bar' file.txt   # matches "bar" only when followed by "foo"

# Named capture (just for demonstration; grep only prints the line)
grep -P '(?<word>[a-z]+)' file.txt

# Case‑insensitive Perl regex
grep -Pi '\bhello\b' file.txt

# Use with other grep options
grep -P -r -l '(?<!foo)bar' /some/directory
```

### TL;DR

- **Syntax:** `grep -P 'your‑perl‑regex' [file…]`
- **Purpose:** Allows you to use the full Perl‑compatible regular‑expression syntax (look‑ahead, look‑behind, named groups, Unicode properties, etc.) inside `grep`.
- **Caveat:** The option is experimental (especially with `-z`) and may warn about unsupported features; for production‑critical regexes you might prefer to run the pattern through Perl directly.

Thus final answer.</think>**Renaming a branch (forcing an overwrite if the target name already exists)**  

| Goal | Command | What it does |
|------|---------|--------------|
| **Rename** (interactive – aborts if the new name is already taken) | ```bash git branch -m <old> <new>``` | Renames the current or specified branch to `<new>`. If `<new>` already exists, Git will refuse and keep both branches. |
| **Rename – force** (overwrites an existing target) | ```bash git branch -M <old> <new>``` | Same as `-m` but **forces** the rename even when `<new>` already exists (the old `<new>` is silently moved out of the way). |
| **Rename while on any branch** | ```bash git branch -m <old> <new>``` (you can be on any branch; the old branch is renamed) | No need to check out the branch first. |

**Deleting a branch (even if it has un‑merged changes)**  

| Goal | Command | What it does |
|------|---------|--------------|
| **Safe delete** (only if the branch is fully merged) | ```bash git branch -d <name>``` | Refuses to delete if the branch has un‑merged commits. |
| **Force delete** (ignores merge status) | ```bash git branch -D <name>``` | Deletes the branch **regardless** of whether its commits are reachable from any other branch or tag. Use with caution. |
| **Delete a remote‑tracking branch** | ```bash git push --delete <remote> <name>```  (or `git push <remote> --delete <name>`) | Removes the branch from the remote repository. |

---

### Quick “one‑liner” example

Suppose you have a local branch `feature‑old` that you want to rename to `feature‑new`, **even if `feature‑new` already exists**, and then delete the original `feature‑old`.

```bash
# 1️⃣ Force‑rename (overwrites any existing feature‑new)
git branch -M feature-old feature-new

# 2️⃣ Force‑delete the old branch (even if it hasn’t been merged)
git branch -D feature-old
```

If you are currently **on** the branch you want to rename, you can omit the old name and Git will rename the checked‑out branch:

```bash
git branch -M feature-new   # renames the current branch to feature-new (force)
git branch -D feature-old   # deletes the now‑non‑existent old name (harmless if already gone)
```

---

### Common pitfalls & tips

| Situation | What to do |
|-----------|------------|
| **You get “fatal: A branch named '<new>' already exists.”** | Use `-M` (capital) instead of `-m` to force the rename. |
| **You want to keep the old branch as a backup before renaming** | Create a copy first: `git copy -c <old> <new>` (Git 2.23+), or `git branch <new>` then `git reset --hard <old>` (careful). |
| **You need to delete a remote branch that is not merged** | `git push <remote> --delete <name>` works regardless of merge status on the remote. |
| **You accidentally deleted a branch you wanted to keep** | You can often recover it with `git reflog` and `git checkout -b <new> <commit>`.** 

---

#### TL;DR

- **Rename (force)** → `git branch -M <old> <new>`  
- **Delete (force, unmerged allowed)** → `git branch -D <name>`  

These two commands give you the ability to rename a branch even when the target name already exists and to delete a branch regardless of its merge state.

---

## 1️⃣ Abort a rebase and go back to the branch you were on

```bash
# While a rebase is in progress
git rebase --abort
```

*What it does*  
- Stops the rebase completely.  
- Resets `HEAD` to where it was **before** the rebase started.  
- Removes the `.git/rebase-merge` (or `.git/rebase-apply`) directory, so you’re back on your normal branch with the working‑tree exactly as it was before you typed `git rebase`.

If you are currently *inside* a rebase and you just want to quit without restoring the original state, you can use:

```bash
git rebase --quit          # leaves you on the branch, but the index is left as‑is
```

But the safe, “reset‑everything” command is `--abort`.

---

## 2️⃣ Check out the original branch after an abort (or if you ended up on a detached HEAD)

In the normal case `git rebase --abort` already switches you back to the branch you rebased onto.  
If for some reason you land on a detached HEAD or you simply want to be certain you’re on the right branch, you can explicit‑ly check it out:

```bash
# Replace <branch-name> with the name of the branch you were on before the rebase
git checkout <branch-name>
```

or, if you only remember that you were on the *current* branch before the rebase started:

```bash
git checkout -          # - always refers to the previous HEAD
```

---

## 3️⃣ Edit the todo list during an **interactive** rebase

### Start the interactive session

```bash
# Rebase the last N commits (replace N with the number you want)
git rebase -i HEAD~N
```

### What the todo‑list looks like

Git opens an editor with a list of commands, one per line, e.g.:

```
pick 1111111 First commit
pick 2222222 Second commit
pick 3333333 Third commit
```

The first word on each line is the **action keyword**.

### Change a “pick” to “edit” (or “e”) so Git pauses at that commit

1. **Find the line** you want to modify (the commit you want to edit).  
2. Replace the leading `pick` with `edit` (you can also use the shortcut `e`).  

   Example – to edit the second commit:

   ```
   pick 1111111 First commit
   edit 2222222 Second commit   ← change `pick` → `edit`
   pick 3333333 Third commit
   ```

3. **Save & quit** the editor. Git will immediately start the rebase and stop right before the marked commit.

### What to do when Git pauses

When the rebase stops, `HEAD` is positioned at the commit you marked for editing, and the working tree reflects that commit’s content.

You can now:

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **Modify files** | `git edit` / `vim` / your favourite editor |
| **Stage changes** | `git add <file>` (or `git add -p` for partial staging) |
| **Amend the commit** | `git commit --amend` (this changes the commit message and/or the snapshot) |
| **Or just continue without amending** | Skip the `commit --amend` step if you only want to tweak the content before the next step |

After you’re happy with the changes:

```bash
# Finish this edited commit and move on to the next one
git rebase --continue
```

If you decide you don’t want to edit that commit any more, you can:

```bash
git rebase --skip          # drop the edited commit and apply the next one
```

or simply abort again:

```bash
git rebase --abort        # start over
```

### Quick cheat‑sheet for common todo‑list edits

| Desired effect | Todo‑list change |
|----------------|------------------|
| **Reorder commits** | Drag / move the lines up/down, then save. |
| **Squash a commit into the previous one** | Change the second commit’s `pick` to `squash` (or `s`). |
| **Drop a commit entirely** | Change its `pick` to `drop` (or `d`). |
| **Edit a commit** | Change its `pick` to `edit` (or `e`). |
| **Fixup (like squash but discard that commit’s message)** | Change to `fixup` (or `f`). |

---

**2. Stop systemctl from ellipsising (truncating) unit names**

System d’s pager truncates long unit names to fit the terminal width.  
You can prevent that in a few ways:

| Goal | Command / Setting | What it does |
|------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Show the full unit name without any truncation** | ```bash\nsystemctl --user list-units --no-legend -o NAME\n``` | `-o NAME` forces the output column to be named *only* the unit name, and `--no‑legend` removes the header/footer so the name isn’t squeezed. |

| **Avoid the pager entirely (good for scripts)** | ```bash\nsystemctl --user list-units --no-legend --no-pager\n``` | `--no-pager` skips the pager altogether; the list is printed directly to stdout. |
| **Inspect a single unit and see its full name** | ```bash\nsystemctl --user show <unit-name>\n``` | `show` prints every property of the unit, including the canonical `Id=` and `Name=` values, which are never ellipsised. |

systemctl --user

# 2️⃣ List all user units with full names
systemctl --user list-units --no-legend -o NAME

# 3️⃣ If you prefer the pager to just print everything
SYSTEMD_PAGER=cat systemctl --user list-units

# 4️⃣ Show full details of one unit (name never truncated)
systemctl --user show nmy-long-unit-name.service
```

---

### Why the ellipsis happens

`systemctl` uses an internal pager (usually `less`) that formats its output to fit the terminal width. When a unit name is longer than the allocated column, the pager truncates it and appends `…`. The options above either bypass the pager (`--no-pager`, `SYSTEMD_PAGER=cat`) or force a single‑column layout (`-o NAME`) where the full name is printed without any width‑truncation.

Running `cargo check --help` lists all available flags, and none of them are named `--fast-mode` or `--fast`. The relevant compilation‑speed options that *are* available are:

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `-r, --release` | Build with release optimizations (usually slower to check, but produces faster binaries). |

If you want `cargo check` to run quickly, the usual approach is one (or a combination) of the following:

1. **Use the default profile** – the default `dev` profile is already optimized for fast iteration (no debug‑info bloat, modest optimizations).
2. **Limit the amount of code being checked** – e.g. `cargo check --bin my_app` instead of `cargo check --all-targets`, or use `--package`/`--lib`/`--bins` to focus on the part you’re working on.
3. **Increase parallelism** – `cargo check -j 4` (or let it default to the number of CPUs) can reduce wall‑clock time on multi‑core machines.
4. **Avoid unnecessary rebuilds** – Cargo’s incremental compilation is already active by default; making sure `Cargo.lock` is up‑to‑date and using `--frozen` can skip network‑related delays.
5. **If you need release‑level optimization but still want a quick check**, you can try `cargo check --release`, but note that this will invoke the full release pipeline and is typically slower than the default dev check.

There isn’t a dedicated `--fast-mode` flag for `cargo check`. The fastest way to check your code is to stick with the default `dev` profile, limit the scope of the check to the parts you’re actively modifying, and let Cargo’s incremental build system handle the rest. texts:
The user asks: "How do I move/rename a branch, even if target exists using git branch?" They want to rename a branch, possibly overwriting an existing target branch. The typical git command to rename a branch is `git branch -m <old> <new>` or `git branch -M <old> <new>` where -M forces even if target exists. The question: "How do I move/rename a branch, even if target exists using git branch?" So answer: use `git branch -M oldname newname`. Explanation: `-M` is shorthand for `--move` and `--force`. It will rename, and if new branch name already exists, it will be replaced. Also can use `git branch -m` (lowercase) which won't force. Provide steps, maybe also alternative using git push with -f. Provide example.

Thus answer: use `git branch -M`. Provide usage. Also mention you need to be on any branch (not necessarily the one being renamed). Provide note about upstream tracking.

Will answer accordingly.</think>Use the **`-M`** (capital‑M) flag with `git branch`.  
`‑M` stands for “move/rename” **and** “force”, so it will rename the branch even if a branch with the target name already exists.

```bash
# Syntax
git branch -M <old‑branch> <new‑branch>
```

### Example

```bash
# Rename 'feature/old' to 'feature/new', overwriting 'feature/new' if it exists
git branch -M feature/old feature/new
```

### What happens

| Situation | Result |
|-----------|--------|
| `<new‑branch>` **does not exist** | The old branch is simply renamed. |
| `<new‑branch>` **exists** | The existing branch is **replaced** (its commit history becomes that of the old branch). |
| You are currently on the branch being renamed | Git will move the branch pointer and you’ll stay on the same commit (now under the new name). |

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `git branch -m <old> <new>` | Rename **without** forcing (fails if `<new>` already exists). |
| `git branch -M <old> <new>` | Rename **forcing** (overwrites `<new>` if it exists). |
| `git branch --move <old> <new>` | Same as `-M` (long form). |

### After renaming

If the branch you just moved was tracking a remote branch, you may want to update the upstream:

```bash
git push -u origin <new‑branch>   # push the new branch
git branch --unset-upstream      # (optional) remove the old tracking info
```

Or, if you want the old remote name to point to the new branch:

```bash
git push -f origin <old‑branch>:<new‑branch>
```

But the core command to force a rename—even when the target already exists—is simply:

```bash
git branch -M old-name new-name
```

or, more compactly, just use `git merge --ff-only` if you only need the fast‑forward guarantee and don’t care about the rebase‑rewritten history.

It tells `journalctl` to truncate (ellipsis‑ize) any field that is longer than the terminal width, instead of printing the full value.

```bash

journalctl --no-full

# Show the last 20 entries with ellipsized fields

```

journalctl --no-full | head -n 5

The man page says: -P, --perl-regexp: Interpret PATTERNS as Perl-compatible regular expressions (PCREs). This option is experimental when combined with -z, and grep -P may warn of unimplemented features.

We can summarize usage: grep -P [options] pattern [file...]. The pattern is a PCRE. Provide examples. Also mention limitations.

We'll answer with explanation and examples.

</think>**`grep -P` / `--perl-regexp`**

| Option | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `-P`, `--perl-regexp` | Treat the pattern(s) that follow as **Perl‑compatible regular expressions (PCREs)** instead of the usual POSIX extended regexes (`-E`) or basic regexes (`-G`). |

### Basic syntax

```bash
grep -P [options] pattern [file…]
```

* `pattern` – any valid PCRE.  
* `options` – the same options you would use with ordinary `grep` (e.g., `-i`, `-r`, `-n`, `-v`, etc.).  
* `file…` – one or more files (or `-` for stdin).  

If you use `-P` together with `-e` or `-f`, the pattern(s) supplied via those options are also interpreted as PCREs.

### Common useful flags (you can combine them with `-P`)

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `-i` | Case‑insensitive matching |
| `-v` | Invert the match (show non‑matching lines) |
| `-n` | Show line numbers |
| `-r` / `-R` | Recurse into directories |
| `-l` | List only filenames that match |
| `-c` | Count matching lines |
| `-m N` | Stop after `N` matches |
| `-z` | Treat binary files as text (note: `-P` with `-z` is **experimental** and may warn) |

### Example usages

1. **Simple PCRE search**

   ```bash
   grep -P '\b[A-Z]{3,}\b' file.txt
   ```
   – Finds any word that consists of **3 or more uppercase letters** (a pattern that would be more cumbersome with POSIX ERE).

2. **Case‑insensitive PCRE with line numbers**

   ```bash
   grep -Pni '\berror\b' logfile
   ```

3. **Recursively search a directory, showing only matching filenames**

   ```bash
   grep -Prl '^#!/usr/bin/env python' /opt/scripts/
   ```

4. **Using `-e` to supply multiple PCREs**

   ```bash
   grep -Pe '^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}' -Pe '^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4}' dates.txt
   ```

5. **Experimental combination with `-z` (null‑byte data)**  

   ```bash
   grep -Pzl 'pattern' *.gz
   ```
   *Warning:* The man page notes that `-P` combined with `-z` is **experimental**; you may see warnings about unimplemented features.

### Things to keep in mind

| Issue | Detail |
|-------|--------|
| **Experimental status** | `-P` is marked “experimental” in the GNU `grep` man page, especially when used with `-z`. Some PCRE features may not be supported, and `grep` may emit warnings. |
| **Portability** | If you need PCRE‑only features (look‑aheads, `\K`, etc.), `-P` is the easiest way, but for maximum portability consider using a dedicated PCRE tool (e.g., `perl -ne '…'` or `pcre2grep`). |
| **Interaction with other regex flags** | `-P` overrides the default basic/extended regex interpretation, so `-E` or `-F` become unnecessary (and are simply ignored). |
| **UTF‑8 / locale** | `grep -P` respects the current locale for character classes like `\w`, `\d`, `\s`. Use `-i` together with `-P` for case‑insensitive matching. |

### Quick cheat‑sheet

```bash
# Basic PCRE search
grep -P '<pattern>' file

# Case‑insensitive
grep -Pi '<pattern>' file

# With line numbers
grep -Pn '<pattern>' file

# Recursive in a directory
grep -Pr '<pattern>' dir/

# Multiple patterns (via -e)
grep -Pe 'pattern1' -Pe 'pattern2' file

# Show only filenames that match
grep -Pl '<pattern>' file(s)
```

If you need more advanced PCRE features that `grep -P` doesn’t support, the typical fallback is to invoke Perl directly, e.g.:

```bash
perl -ne 'print if /<pattern>/)' file
```

but for most everyday pattern‑matching tasks `grep -P` works nicely and follows the same syntax as the rest of `grep`.

Or maybe they want to use git commit -S? Not sure.

We can interpret: They want to create a commit that includes a diff patch with context lines. Maybe they want to use git commit with -c message and include diff stats? Or use git commit -v which shows the diff being committed.

Alternatively, they might be asking: "How do I generate diffs with n lines context using git diff?" But they wrote "using git commit". Could be a misunderstanding.

We can answer: Use git diff -U<n> to set context lines, and then you can commit using git commit with that diff via git apply or git am. Or use git commit -F <file> to commit from a diff file.

Better to clarify: If you want the commit message to include a diff with context, you can generate a diff with git diff -U<n> > patch.txt, then git commit -F patch.txt. Or use git commit -v to show diff during commit.

We can also mention using git format-patch -U<n>.

Let's ask for clarification? Probably we should answer with methods.

We can also show command: git diff -U5 > changes.patch then git commit -F changes.patch.

Or use git commit with --diff-option? Not exist.

Thus answer: Use git diff -U<n> to create patch with context lines, then apply and commit.

We'll provide steps.

</think>Below are the common ways to get a **diff that contains ` <n>` lines of context** and then turn that diff into a commit.  
The core Git command that controls the amount of context is `git diff -U<n>` (“‑U” stands for “unified context”).  

---

## 1. Generate a patch with ` <n>` context lines

```bash
# Show the last commit’s changes (or any range) with N lines of context
git diff -U<n> <commit‑ish>..<commit‑ish> > my‑patch.patch
```

*Examples*

```bash
# 3 lines of context for the diff between the last two commits
git diff -U3 HEAD~1..HEAD > 2‑commit‑diff.patch

# 5 lines of context for all unstaged changes
git diff -U5 > unstaged‑changes.patch
```

The resulting `my‑patch.patch` will look like a normal unified diff, but each hunk will be prefixed/reversed with `+`, `-`, and the surrounding `context` lines (the lines that stay unchanged). The number of those context lines is exactly ` <n> ` (or up to the total number of lines available if the file is shorter).

---

## 2. Commit the patch

There are a few ways to turn that patch into a commit, depending on your workflow.

### A. `git apply` + `git commit` (most explicit)

```bash
# 1️⃣ Apply the patch to the working tree
git apply my-patch.patch   # this modifies files in the work‑tree

# 2️⃣ Stage the changed files
git add .                 # or `git add <file>` for specific paths

# 3️⃣ Record the commit (you can keep the default message or edit it)
git commit -m "Your commit message here"
```

*Why this works*: `git apply` respects the context lines and only applies the actual changes (`+`/`-` lines). The context is discarded after the patch is applied, but the diff you generated still contains the ` <n>` context you asked for.

---

### B. `git commit -F` (commit from a file)

If you already have a patch file and want Git to read the commit message from it (the first line of the file becomes the commit message, the rest is ignored), you can do:

```bash
git commit -F my-patch.patch
```

*Tip*: The patch file must be a **unified diff** (the output of `git diff -U<n>`). Git will parse the `+`/`-` lines, apply them, and automatically create a commit. If you also want the commit message to include a summary, add a one‑line header before the diff:

```
Add new feature X

--- (rest of the diff follows)
```

---

### C. `git am` (apply a mailbox‑style patch)

When the patch was produced by `git format-patch` (or manually), you can feed it directly to `git am`:

```bash
git am my-patch.patch
```

`git am` will:
1. Parse the unified diff (respecting the context lines).
2. Prompt you for a commit message (or use the message embedded in the patch, if any).
3. Create the commit.

---

## 3. Quick cheat‑sheet

| Goal | Command | What it does |
|------|---------|--------------|
| **Create a diff with N context lines** | `git diff -U<N> <range> > patch.txt` | Writes a unified diff where each hunk shows `N` lines of context before/after the changes. |
| **Apply that diff and commit** | `git apply patch.txt && git add . && git commit -m "msg"` | Applies the changes, stages them, and records a commit. |
| **Commit directly from the patch (message from first line)** | `git commit -F patch.txt` | Reads the patch, applies it, and uses the first line as the commit message. |
| **Patch produced by `format-patch` already has context** | `git format-patch -U<N> <range>` | Generates a series of `.patch` files, each with `N` context lines, ready for `git am` or `git apply`. |

---

## 4. Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

| Problem | Why it happens | Fix |

The user asks: "How do I move/rename a branch, even if target exists using git branch?" They want to rename a branch, possibly overwriting an existing target branch. The typical git command to rename a branch is `git branch -m <old> <new>`. The `-m` flag will move/rename, and if the new branch name already exists, by default it will error out. To force overwrite, you can use `-M` (uppercase) which is equivalent to `--move --force`. So the answer: use `git branch -M oldname newname`. This will rename, and if target exists, it will delete the old target and rename. Alternatively, you can first delete the target branch `git branch -D newname` then rename. But the question specifically "even if target exists using git branch". So answer: use `git branch -M`. Provide explanation.

We can also mention that `git branch -m` (lowercase) will error if target exists. So the solution: `git branch -M <old> <new>`.

We can optionally show how to do via `git rename`? but not needed.

Thus answer: use `git branch -M old new`. Provide nuance.

We can also verify by running a quick test in a git repo, but not needed.

We'll respond with explanation.</think>**Use the upper‑case `-M` flag**  

```bash
git branch -M <old‑branch> <new‑branch>
```

- `-M` stands for **move/rename** *and* **force**.  
- If `<new‑branch>` already exists, Git will silently replace it (the old one is deleted and the name is moved to the current checkout).  
- Without the upper‑case flag (`git branch -m …`) Git will error out when the target name is already taken.

### Quick comparison

| Command | Behaviour if target exists |
|---------|----------------------------|
| `git branch -m old new`   | **Error**: “fatal: A branch named 'new' already exists.” |
| `git branch -M old new`   | **Force rename**: the existing `new` is overwritten, `old` is renamed to `new`. |
| `git branch -a` (list)    | Just lists branches – no effect. |

### Example

```bash
# Rename 'feature' to 'feature‑v2', even if 'feature‑v2' already exists
git branch -M feature feature-v2
```

If you want to be extra safe you can first delete the old target:

```bash
git branch -D feature-v2   # force‑delete the existing branch
git branch -M feature feature-v2   # then rename
```

But the single‑command `git branch -M` is the direct way to rename **even when the target already exists**.

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

           When specified, this option clears all previous --decorate-refs or
           --decorate-refs-exclude options and relaxes the default decoration filter to include all

           to all.

           Print out the ref name given on the command line by which each commit was reached.

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

           --decorate-refs-exclude options and relaxes the default decoration filter to include all

Will answer accordingly.</think>The `journalctl` command can attach the *message explanations* that are stored in the system catalog (the “systemd‑catalog” package).  
The flag that turns this on is **`-x`** (or the long form **`--catalog`**).

```bash
# Show journal entries with their built‑in explanations
journalctl -x

# (or the explicit long form)
journalctl --catalog
```

You can combine the catalog flag with any of the usual filters, e.g.:

```bash
# Explanations for the sshd service only
journalctl -u sshd -x

# Explanations for the current boot
journalctl -b -x

# Explanations for a date range
journalctl -S "2024‑01-01" -U "2024‑01‑02" -x
```

### What the flag does

- **`-x` / `--catalog`** looks up each log message in the system catalog and, if an explanation is available, prints it after the message text.  
- The catalog contains human‑readable descriptions for many of the messages that systemd produces (e.g., “Started / stopped …”, “Failed to …”, etc.).  
- If no explanation is found for a particular message, `journalctl` simply prints the message without extra text.

### Quick test

```bash
journalctl -x | head -n 20
```

You’ll see lines similar to:

```
-- Reboot --
Jan 01 00:00:01 hostname systemd[1]: Started Session c1 of user root.
Jan 01 00:00:01 hostname systemd[1]: /etc/systemd/system/getty.service:10: Deprecated syntax, use ExecStart=
Jan 01 00:00:01 hostname systemd[1]: [GETTY] Ignoring obsolete unit
```

The second column (or the trailing text after the message) is the catalog explanation, when one exists.

---

**Tip:** The catalog is part of the `systemd` package, so make sure it’s installed/up‑to‑date (`sudo dnf/yum/pacman -Sy systemd` or `sudo apt-get install systemd`) if you don’t see any explanations.

We can answer: Use `git diff --stat` shows diffstat, and `--find-renames` or `-M` to detect renames. Combine: `git diff --stat -M` or `git diff --stat --find-renames=...`. Also can use `git diff --stat --diff-filter=R` maybe. Actually `-M` is for rename detection. Also `--stat` shows summary with inserted/deleted lines and files.

Thus answer: `git diff -M --stat` or `git diff --stat -M`. Also can use `git diff --stat --find-renames=exact` etc.

We can also mention `git diff --stat -C` (copy detection) and `-R` (rearrange). But main is `-M`.

We can also show example.

Thus answer.

Probably no need to use tools.

But maybe we should verify via bash? Could run `git diff --help` but not needed.

We'll answer directly.

</think>**Short answer**

```bash
git diff -M --stat
# or the equivalent long form
git diff --find-renames= --stat
```

- **`-M`** (or **`--find-renames`**) tells Git to detect *renames* (and copies, with `-C`).  
- **`--stat`** (or **`-stat`**) makes `git diff` output a *diffstat* summary – a line‑by‑line count of inserted / deleted lines per file, without showing the actual patch.

You can combine them in any order; the most common forms are:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `git diff -M --stat` | Detect renames **and** show the diffstat. |
| `git diff --stat -M` | Same as above (order doesn’t matter). |
| `git diff --find-renames= --stat` | Long‑form equivalent. |
| `git diff -C --stat` | Also detects *copies* in addition to renames. |
| `git diff --stat --summary` | Shows the same diffstat plus a short “summary” line (files changed, insertions, deletions). |

**Explanation of the flags**

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-M` / `--find-renames` | Enables rename detection. Git looks at the content of files and, if a file’s content appears in another path, it reports it as a rename (old → new). You can fine‑tune the similarity threshold with `--find-renames=` options (e.g., `--find-renames=80%` requires at least 80 % similarity). |
| `-C` / `--find-copies` | In addition to renames, also detects files that were copied and then modified. Use `-C` if you want copy detection as well. |

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.

</think>`systemctl` itself doesn’t have a dedicated “package‑version” command, but the unit files that systemd manages often contain a **`Version=`** tag that the distributing package sets when it installs the unit. You can pull that value out with the `show` sub‑command and the `-p` (property) flag.

---

## 1. Show the `Version` property of a single unit  

```bash
systemctl show <unit-name> -p Version
```

* `<unit-name>` – the name of the unit **without** the “.service” suffix (systemctl will add it automatically).  
* If the unit file defines `Version=1.4.2` the command prints exactly that line; otherwise you’ll get `Version=` with an empty value.

**Example**

```bash
$ systemctl show nginx.service -p Version
Version=1.24.0
```

---

## 2. Display the whole unit file (you’ll see the Version line among other directives)

```bash
systemctl cat <unit-name>
```

This prints the complete unit file that systemd loaded, so you can verify the `Version=` line (or any other custom tag the packager added).

**Example**

```bash
$ systemctl cat nginx.service
#  This file is part of systemd.
...
[Unit]
Description=nginx - high performance HTTP server
Version=1.24.0
...
```

---

## 3. List all installed unit files and their `Version` tags (if any)

```bash
systemctl list-unit-files -p Version
```

(Note: the `-p` flag works with `list-unit-files` as of systemd 254+; it shows the value of the requested property for each unit file.)

---

## 4. When the `Version` tag is missing  

If the unit file doesn’t contain a `Version=` line, `systemctl` can’t give you the package version directly. In that case you’ll have to fall back to the native package manager:

| Distribution | Command |
|--------------|---------|
| **Debian / Ubuntu** | `dpkg -S $(systemctl show <unit>.service -p Into) ` or `apt-cache policy <package>` |
| **RHEL / CentOS / Fedora** | `rpm -q <package>` (the package name is often the same as the unit name minus the “.service” suffix) |
| **Arch Linux** | `pacman -Q <package>` |

You can usually discover the package name from the unit file’s `Vendor=` or `Comment=` fields, or from the path shown in `systemctl status <unit>` (e.g., `Loaded: loaded … /usr/lib/systemd/system/<unit>.service`).

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **Get the `Version` tag** | `systemctl show <unit> -p Version` |
| **View the whole unit file** | `systemctl cat <unit>` |
| **List all unit files with their `Version`** | `systemctl list-unit-files -p Version` |
| **Find the installing package** | `rpm -q <package>` / `dpkg -S <file>` (after you identify the package from the unit) |

So, to answer your original question: **use `systemctl show <unit-name> -p Version`** (or `systemctl cat <unit-name>` to inspect the file) – that’s the way systemd exposes the package version it stored in the unit file. If the tag isn’t present, you’ll need to query the system’s package manager directly.

The --perl-regexp (-P) option interprets patterns as Perl-compatible regular expressions (PCRE). The syntax is the same as Perl regex, but with some limitations (experimental). We can summarize usage: grep -P [options] pattern [file]. Also mention that it's experimental with -z. Provide examples.

We'll answer based on the man page.</think>**`grep --perl-regexp` (‑ `‑P`)**  

| Option | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `-P`, `--perl-regexp` | *Interpret the pattern(s) as **Perl‑compatible regular expressions** (PCRE).* The pattern syntax is the same as you would write in Perl (character classes, look‑ahead/look‑behind, capture groups, back‑references, etc.).* |

### Basic syntax

```bash
grep -P [options] pattern [file…]
```

or, when you want to use the option together with other grep flags:

```bash
grep -P -e 'pattern' [file…]
grep -P -f patternfile [file…]
```

### What the pattern language can do

- **Extended regex features** (`|`, `?`, `+`, `{}`, etc.) – already available with `-E`/`--extended-regexp`.
- **PCRE‑only extensions**:  
  - Look‑ahead `(?=…)` and look‑behind `(?<=…)`
  - Named capture groups `(?<name>…)` and back‑references `\1`, `\2`, …
  - Possessive quantifiers `++`, `+?`, etc.
  - `\d`, `\D`, `\w`, `\W`, `\s`, `\S`, `\b`, `\B`
  - Recursive patterns `(?R)` or `(?0)`
  - Many more Perl‑specific constructs

(See the *PCRE* documentation for the complete set of supported atoms and operators.)

### Things to keep in mind

1. **Experimental status** – The grep manual notes that `-P` is **experimental**, especially when combined with `-z` (`--null-data`). Some patterns that are valid in Perl may cause a warning or be rejected.
2. **Unicode support** – `grep -P` works with UTF‑8 strings, but the handling can differ from pure Perl depending on the locale and the version of the PCRE library installed on your system.
3. **Performance** – PCRE matching is generally a little slower than the default POSIX‑ERE matching, so use `-P` only when you need the extra Perl‑compatible features.
4. **Compatibility** – If you are writing a script that must be portable across systems, consider staying with `-E` (extended regex) or `-G` (basic regex) and only fall back to `-P` for the specific constructs you need.

### Quick examples

```bash
# Match a word that is followed by a literal “(foo)”
grep -P '\b\w+(?=\(foo\))' file.txt

# Match a line that contains a decimal number (one or more digits)
grep -P '\d+' file.txt

# Use a capture group to extract part of the match
grep -Po '\d+' file.txt   # -o prints only the matching part

# Combine with other options
grep -P -i 'hello.*world' file.txt   # case‑insensitive Perl regex
```

### Summary

- **Syntax**: `grep -P pattern [file…]` (or `-P` combined with other grep flags).
- **Pattern language**: Full PCRE syntax – everything you can write in Perl regular expressions.
- **Caveat**: Experimental; may warn or fail with obscure patterns or with `-z`. Use it when you need PCRE features that `-E`/`-G` don’t provide.

Will answer.</think>**Short answer**

- **Force‑rename (even if the target name already exists):**  

  ```bash
  git branch -M <old‑branch> <new‑branch>
  ```

- **Normal rename (fails if the target already exists):**  

  ```bash
  git branch -m <old‑branch> <new‑branch>
  ```

*`-M`* is short for “‑m --force”.  It moves the branch pointer to the new name and, if `<new‑branch>` already exists, it is **deleted** first (the old pointer is simply moved).  

If you prefer the interactive, non‑destructive way, delete the target first and then rename:

```bash
# Delete the target branch (‑D = force delete even if unmerged)
git branch -D <new‑branch>      # or git branch -d <new‑branch> if you’re sure it’s merged

# Rename the source branch
git branch -m <old‑branch> <new‑branch>
```

---

### Why the two commands exist

| Command | Behaviour when `<new‑branch>` already exists |
|---------|----------------------------------------------|
| `git branch -m <old> <new>` | **Error**: “fatal: A branch named '<new>' already exists.” |
| `git branch -M <old> <new>` | **Force rename**: the existing `<new>` is silently deleted and `<old>` is renamed to `<new>`. |
| `git branch <old> <new>` (no flag) | Same as `-m` – will not overwrite. |

The force flag is useful when you want to “swap” names or when you’re sure you want the old branch’s history to replace the existing one.

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

```bash
# 1️⃣ Normal rename (will error if target exists)
git branch -m old-name new-name

# 2️⃣ Force rename (overwrites existing target)
git branch -M old-name new-name

# 3️⃣ Rename after deleting the target manually
git branch -D new-name          # delete if you no longer need it
git branch -m old-name new-name

# 4️⃣ Move a branch to a different commit (keeps the name)
git branch -f old-name <commit‑ish>
```

---

### How to verify

```bash
# List all branches and note the new name
git branch -a

# Or see the reflog for the old name – it should now point to the same commit as the new name
git log --oneline old-name   # (if you still have a ref; otherwise just check new-name)
```

That’s it! Use `git branch -M` when you need the rename to succeed regardless of an existing target, or delete the target first and use `git branch -m` for a safer, non‑destructive rename.
