GIT-DIFF(1)                                  Git Manual                                 GIT-DIFF(1)

NAME
       git-diff - Show changes between commits, commit and working tree, etc

SYNOPSIS
       git diff [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [<commit>...] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <commit>...<commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <blob> <blob>
       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Show changes between the working tree and the index or a tree, changes between the index and
       a tree, changes between two trees, changes resulting from a merge, changes between two blob
       objects, or changes between two files on disk.

       git diff [<options>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you made relative to the index (staging area for the
           next commit). In other words, the differences are what you could tell Git to further add
           to the index but you still haven’t. You can stage these changes by using git-add(1).

       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]
           This form is to compare the given two paths on the filesystem. You can omit the
           --no-index option when running the command in a working tree controlled by Git and at
           least one of the paths points outside the working tree, or when running the command
           outside a working tree controlled by Git. This form implies --exit-code. If both paths
           point to directories, additional pathspecs may be provided. These will limit the files
           included in the difference. All such pathspecs must be relative as they apply to both
           sides of the diff.

       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you staged for the next commit relative to the named
           <commit>. Typically you would want comparison with the latest commit, so if you do not
           give <commit>, it defaults to HEAD. If HEAD does not exist (e.g. unborn branches) and
           <commit> is not given, it shows all staged changes.  --staged is a synonym of --cached.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --cached --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff --cached $(git
           merge-base A HEAD).

       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you have in your working tree relative to the named
           <commit>. You can use HEAD to compare it with the latest commit, or a branch name to
           compare with the tip of a different branch.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff $(git merge-base A HEAD).

       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> <commit> [--] [<path>...]
           This is to view the changes between two arbitrary <commit>.

           If --merge-base is given, use the merge base of the two commits for the "before" side.
           git diff --merge-base A B is equivalent to git diff $(git merge-base A B) B.

       git diff [<options>] <commit> <commit>...<commit> [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the results of a merge commit. The first listed <commit> must be

           ways to produce the desired set of revisions are to use the suffixes @ and ^!. If A is a
           merge commit, then git diff A A^@, git diff A^! and git show A all give the same
           combined diff.

So we need options: -p or --patch for patch format, and -C or --copy for copy detection, maybe -B for blank, -M for move, -S for content, etc. The question: "output patch format, and detect copies, in the same command". So answer: use git diff -p -C (or --patch --copy). Also maybe -C -C? Actually -C detects copies as well as moves. There's also --find-copies-harder for more thorough detection, used with -C. So command: git diff -p -C or git diff --patch --copy. Also can combine with --stat, etc.

We should provide explanation and example. Might also mention -R? But answer: -p/--patch outputs patch; -C/--copy detects copies; -C --find-copies-harder for full tree comparison.

We can also show a sample command: git diff -p -C --find-copies-harder.

Thus final answer.</think>**Git diff options you can combine in a single command**

| Goal | Option(s) | What it does |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| **Output the diff in “patch” format** (i.e. the unified‑diff that shows `---`, `+++`, context lines, and hunks) | `-p`  or `--patch` | Prints the classic patch representation of the changes. |
| **Detect copies** (as well as moves) | `-C` or `--copy` | Shows any source file that was copied (or moved) into the changed file, annotating the patch with `copy from <path>`. |
| **Aggressive copy detection** (examines the whole history, not just the current index/tree) | `-C` + `--find‑copies‑harder` | In addition to the fast “copy‑from‑index” check, Git will scan the full object database for potential copies. This can be slower but finds copies that span branches or older commits. |

### One‑liner that does both

```bash
git diff -p -C           # basic copy detection
# or, if you want the extra‑thorough scan:
git diff -p -C --find-copies-harder
```

Both commands produce a unified‑diff patch **and** will annotate any lines that Git identifies as being copied from another path (or from an earlier version of the same file). The `‑C` flag works for `git diff` between any two trees, commits, or the working tree and a commit.

### Quick examples

```bash
# Show the patch for the working‑tree vs. HEAD, with copy detection
git diff -p -C

# Show the patch for two arbitrary commits, with aggressive copy detection
git diff -p -C --find-copies-harder v1.2 v1.3
```

### What the output looks like

```
--- a/file.txt
+++ b/file.txt
@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@
 line 1
 line 2
+line 3'  ← new line
 copy from b/other.txt   ← added by -C
```

The `copy from …` line appears **only** when Git is confident that the surrounding hunk matches an existing file elsewhere in the tree/commit being compared.

---

**Bottom line:**  
`-p` (or `--patch`) gives you the patch format, and `-C` (or `--copy`) adds copy‑/move detection. Adding `--find‑copies‑harder` makes the copy search more exhaustive. You can safely combine them in a single `git diff` invocation.

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

       --no-decorate, --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]
           Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown. Possible values are:

               `short`;; the ref name prefixes `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/` and
                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.
               `full`;; the full ref name (including prefix) is printed.
               `auto`:: if the output is going to a terminal, the ref names
                       are shown as if `short` were given, otherwise no ref names are
                       shown.

           The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value
           of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto.

       --decorate-refs=<pattern>, --decorate-refs-exclude=<pattern>
           For each candidate reference, do not use it for decoration if it matches any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs-exclude or if it doesn’t match any of the
           <pattern> parameters given to --decorate-refs. The log.excludeDecoration config option
           allows excluding refs from the decorations, but an explicit --decorate-refs pattern will
           override a match in log.excludeDecoration.

           If none of these options or config settings are given, then references are used as
           decoration if they match HEAD, refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, refs/stash/, or refs/tags/.

       --clear-decorations
           When specified, this option clears all previous --decorate-refs or
           --decorate-refs-exclude options and relaxes the default decoration filter to include all
           references. This option is assumed if the config value log.initialDecorationSet is set
           to all.

       --source
           Print out the ref name given on the command line by which each commit was reached.

       --mailmap, --no-mailmap, --use-mailmap, --no-use-mailmap
           Use mailmap file to map author and committer names and email address

texts:
The user asks: "With git diff, how do I detect renames, and also show diffstat instead of patch?" They want to know git diff options to detect renames and show diffstat (summary stats) instead of the full patch.

We can answer: Use `git diff --stat` to show diffstat, and `--name-status` maybe. To detect renames, use `-M` or `--renames`. Combined: `git diff -M --stat` or `git diff --stat --renames`. Actually `git diff` default does not show renames; you need `-M` or `--renames=...`. Also `--stat` shows summary with insertions, deletions, and file names. To also show rename detection, you can use `git diff -M --stat`. Or `git diff --stat -M`. Additionally, you can use `--diff-filter=R` maybe.

We can also mention `--stat` shows a line per file with number of changes and path, and if rename detected it shows `=>` old name -> new name.

We can also mention `git diff --stat --summary` maybe.

We can optionally show an example command.

Thus answer: Use `git diff -M --stat` or `git diff --stat -M`. Also can use `--no-index` etc.

We can also mention that `git diff --stat` shows diffstat but not rename detection; combine with `-M`.

We can also mention that `git diff --stat --find-renames` maybe.

We should answer concisely.

Check if need to use tool? Not needed; it's general knowledge.

Thus final answer.</think>**Combine the two options in a single `git diff` invocation**

| Goal | Option | Example |
|------|--------|---------|
| Show a *diffstat* (summary of insertions / deletions / file names) | `--stat` | `git diff --stat` |
| Detect *renames* and show the old‑name → new‑name arrow (`=>`) | `-M` (or `--renames`) | `git diff -M` |
| **Both together** | `-M --stat` (or `--stat -M`) | `git diff -M --stat` |

```bash
# Show diffstat and rename detection
git diff -M --stat
```

**What you’ll see**

```
 diff --git a/old_file.txt b/new_file.txt
 index 1234567..abcdefg 100644
--- a/old_file.txt
+++ b/new_file.txt
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
-old line
+new line
@@ -10,3 +10,3 @@
 ...
--- /dev/null b/new_file.txt
+++ /dev/null b/new_file.txt
@@ -1,0 +1,3 @@
+new file
 
 rename old_file.txt => new_file.txt
```

The last line (`rename old_file.txt => new_file.txt`) appears only when the `-M` rename‑detection flag is active. The preceding lines (the usual `diff` output) are suppressed when you use `--stat`; instead you get a one‑line summary per path, e.g.:

```
 new_file.txt | 3 +++
 old_file.txt | 3 --- 
```

**Other useful flags**

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `--stat` | Shows total insertions/deletions and the changed file names (no patch). |
| `-M` / `--renames` | Enables rename detection. |
| `-C` / `--copies` | Also detects copies (useful when a file is duplicated and modified). |
| `--stat --summary` | Same as `--stat` but adds a short header with “X files changed, Y insertions(+), Z deletions(-)”. |
| `--no-index` | Allows diffing files that are not tracked by git (useful for quick comparisons). |

**Quick cheat‑sheet**

```bash
# Basic rename‑aware diffstat
git diff -M --stat

# Also show copies
git diff -MC --stat

# Human‑readable summary only (no patch lines)
git diff --stat --summary
```

Just prepend `-M` (or `--renames`) to any `git diff` command that already uses `--stat`, and git will both detect renames and present the concise diffstat view.

texts:
We need to answer how to move/rename a branch, even if target exists using git branch. The user asks: "How do I move/rename a branch, even if target exists using git branch?" They likely want to rename a branch, possibly force overwrite if target branch already exists. The command `git branch -m` can rename a branch, but if target exists, it refuses unless you use `-M` (capital M) which forces rename even if target exists. So answer: use `git branch -M <old> <new>` or `git branch -m <old> <new>` for interactive. Also can delete and recreate. Provide steps.

We can also check git docs via bash maybe, but not needed. Provide explanation.

Thus final answer: use `git branch -M old new`. Explanation.

Will respond.</think>**Use the “force‑rename” flag (`-M`) on `git branch`.**  

```bash
# Rename <old‑branch> to <new‑branch>, overwriting <new‑branch> if it already exists
git branch -M <old-branch> <new-branch>
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-m` (lower‑case) | Interactive rename. If the target branch already exists, Git aborts with an error. |
| `-M` (upper‑case) | **Force rename**. Moves the branch to the new name **even if** a branch with that name already exists (it will be replaced). |

### Example

```bash
# Suppose you have a branch called "feature‑old" and you want to rename it to "feature‑new",
# but "feature‑new" already exists.
git branch -M feature-old feature-new
```

Running the command above will:

1. Rename `feature‑old` to `feature‑new`.
2. If `feature‑new` already existed, its old contents are **discarded** and the new branch now points to the same commit that `feature‑old` was pointing at.
3. The original `feature‑old` branch is deleted.

### What if you only want to move the branch when the target does **not** exist?

Use the lower‑case `-m` (or just omit the flag, since `git branch <old> <new>` defaults to a move, but it will error if the target exists):

```bash
git branch -m feature-old feature-new   # aborts if feature-new already exists
```

### Alternative (manual) approach

If you prefer not to use the force flag, you can achieve the same result with three ordinary commands:

```bash
# 1. Create the new branch at the same commit as the old one
git branch <new-branch> <old-branch>

# 2. Delete the old branch (‑D forces deletion even if it’s not fully merged)
git branch -D <old-branch>

# 3. (Optional) Push the new branch wherever you need it
git push origin <new-branch>
```

But the single‑command `-M` method is the most concise when you *do* want to overwrite an existing target.

| **Edit / amend the current commit** | `edit` (or `e`) | Git stops after that commit so you can `git commit --amend` (or make any other changes) and then run `git rebase --continue`. |

---

## 1. The interactive‑rebase todo list

When you run

```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~N   # or any other revision range
```

Git opens an editor with a list like this (newest commit at the top):

```
pick abc123 First commit
pick def456 Second commit
pick 789abc Third commit
```

Each line starts with a **verb** that tells Git what to do:

| Verb | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `pick` (or `p`) | Use the commit as‑is. |
| `edit` (or `e`) | **Stop** before applying this commit so you can modify it. |
| `skip` (Git 2.20+) | **Omit** this commit entirely. |
| `drop` (or `d`) | **Remove** this commit (same as `skip` but older syntax). |
| `squash` (or `s`) | Merge this commit into the previous one, but keep the commit message for editing. |
| `fixup` (or `f`) | Merge this commit into the previous one, **discarding** its commit message. |

You can change any verb by editing the line in the file, saving & quitting. Git will then apply the list accordingly.

---

## 2. “Edit the todo list” – what that actually means

* **Changing `pick` → `edit`**  
  - Git pauses right before the commit is applied.  
  - You get a shell prompt where you can run `git commit --amend`, add files, reset, etc.  
  - When you’re happy, run `git rebase --continue` (or `git rebase --abort` to cancel).

* **Changing `pick` → `skip` / `drop`**  
  - Git **skips** that commit and proceeds to the next one.  
  - No shell prompt appears; the rebase continues automatically (or you can still run `git rebase --continue` to move on manually).

* **Editing the whole file**  
  - You may want to *both* edit some commits **and** skip others.  
  - Just edit each line accordingly, save, and Git will execute the list in order.

There is **no flag you pass to `git rebase -i` that simultaneously turns a commit into “edit” *and* “skip”**. The verb for each commit is set *individually* in the todo list.

I'll keep it concise.</think>`grep -P` (or `--perl-regexp`) tells **grep** to interpret the pattern as a **Perl‑compatible regular expression** (PCRE).  
The syntax is that of Perl regular expressions, which is a superset of the POSIX extended regex syntax used by `grep -E`.

### Basic syntax (same as `grep -E`)

| Construct | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `.`       | any single character |
| `^`       | start of line |
| `$`       | end of line |
| `*`       | zero or more of the preceding element |
| `+``      | one or more of the preceding element |
| `?`       | zero or one of the preceding element |
| `{m,n}`   | at least *m* and at most *n* repetitions |
| `[…]`     | character class |
| `[^…]`    | negated character class |
| `(…)`     | grouping |
| `|`       | alternation (OR) |
| `\b`      | word boundary |
| `\d`      | any digit |
| `\s`      | any whitespace |
| `\w`      | any word character (letter, digit, underscore) |

### Perl‑specific extensions

| Feature | Syntax | Example |
|---------|--------|---------|
| **Lookahead** (assertion) | `(?=pattern)` | `grep -P 'foo(?=bar)'` matches “foo” only when followed by “bar”. |
| **Lookbehind** | `(?<=pattern)` | `grep -P '(?<=bar)foo'` matches “foo” only when preceded by “bar”. |
| **Named capture group** | `(?<name>pattern)` | `grep -P '(?<year>\d{4})'` and later retrieve `${year}` (only useful with `grep -oP`). |
| **Non‑capturing group** | `(?:pattern)` | Groups without saving the matched text. |
| **Possessive quantifier** | `+?`, `*?`, `??` | Matches greedily but won’t backtrack (rarely needed). |
| **Unicode property escapes** | `\p{Prop}` | `\p{L}` matches any Unicode letter, `\p{N}` any numeric digit, etc. |

### Typical usage

```bash
# Simple Perl‑regexp search (case‑insensitive)
grep -Pi 'hello world' file.txt

# Match “foo” only when followed by “bar”
grep -P 'foo(?=bar)' file.txt

# Extract a four‑digit year and print only that part
grep -Po '\d{4}' file.txt   # -o prints only the matching part

# Match a word at the beginning of a line (Perl ^ anchors the start)
grep -P '^\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}' file.txt   # SSN pattern
```

### Quick cheat‑sheet

```
grep -P 'PATTERN' file
```

- `-P` – treat PATTERN as a Perl regex.  
- `-i` – ignore case (works with Perl regexps).  
- `-o` – output only the matched text (very useful with Perl regexps).  
- `-e 'PATTERN'` – when you need to pass the pattern via the command line (otherwise you can just write the pattern as the first argument).

If you need the full Perl regex grammar, the `perlre` man page or the online perldoc is the definitive reference, but for most everyday tasks the table above covers the essentials.

To find package that provides the service, you can use `systemctl show -p Id` etc. Maybe better to suggest using `pacman -Q` on Arch, `apt-cache policy` on Debian, etc. Given the question, I'd answer: systemctl itself doesn't display package version; you need to query the package manager. It is designed to control the system manager and show runtime state (status, start‑up, etc.), not package metadata. However, you can combine `systemctl` with your distribution’s package manager to find the version. Below are the most common ways, depending on the Linux distribution you are using. --- ## 1. Find the binary that the unit runs → query the package 1. **Show the unit file** (contains the executable path) ```bash systemctl cat ``` Example: `systemctl cat sshd.service` 2. **Locate the binary** that appears in the output (look for the `ExecStart=` line). Suppose the binary is `/usr/sbin/sshd`. 3. **Query the package that owns that binary** using your distro’s package manager: | Distribution | Command to show package version | |--------------|---------------------------------| | **Debian / Ubuntu** | `dpkg -S /usr/sbin/sshd` → `dpkg -s ` for version
or simply `dpkg -s openssh-server | grep Version` | | **RHEL / CentOS / AlmaLinux / Rocky** | `rpm -qf /usr/sbin/sshd` (query file) → `rpm -q ` for version | | **Arch Linux** | `pacman -Qo /usr/sbin/sshd` (owns file) → `pacman -Q ` for version | | **Fedora / openSUSE** | `dnf repoquery --file /usr/sbin/sshd` or `rpm -qf /usr/sbin/sshd` | | **Gentoo** | `equery which /usr/sbin/sshd` → `emerge --info` or `q ` | **Example (Debian/Ubuntu):** ```bash # 1. Show the unit file systemctl cat ssh.service # 2. Extract the binary path (e.g., /usr/sbin/sshd) # 3. Query the package dpkg -S /usr/sbin/sshd # shows: openssh-server: /usr/sbin/sshd dpkg -s openssh-server # shows Version: 1:9.5p1-4ubuntu1 ``` **Example (RHEL‑based):** ```bash systemctl cat wpa_supplicant.service # shows ExecStart=/usr/sbin/wpa_supplicant ... rpm -qf /usr/sbin/wpa_supplicant # shows wpa_supplicant-2.10-1.el8 ``` --- ## 2. One‑liner (distro‑specific) if you already know the unit name If you just want a quick “guess” and your distro systemd units are named after the package (e.g., `nginx.service`, `postgresql.service`), you can often directly query the package: | Distro | One‑liner | |--------|-----------| | **Debian/Ubuntu** | `systemctl status nginx | grep -i version` **won’t work**; instead `dpkg -s nginx | grep Version` | | **RHEL/CentOS/Fedora** | `systemctl status firewalld` → then `rpm -q firewalld` | | **Arch** | `systemctl status docker` → then `pacman -Q docker` | In practice, the **two‑step** method (show unit → find binary → query package) is the most reliable across all distributions. --- ## 3. If you only need the *unit* version (not the package) Some units expose a custom `Version=` property that the administrator set (rare). You can view it with: ```bash systemctl show -p Version ``` But this **does not** reflect the installed package version; it’s just a free‑form string you (or a vendor) may have added. --- ## TL;DR - `systemctl` alone cannot show the package version. - Use `systemctl cat ` → get the binary path → query your distro’s package manager (`dpkg`, `rpm`, `pacman`, etc.) for the version. - If you’re on a Debian‑based system: `dpkg -S $(systemctl cat | grep ExecStart | awk '{print $2}')` (or simply `dpkg -s `). - On RHEL‑based: `rpm -qf $(systemctl cat | grep ExecStart | awk '{print $2}')`. * `docker images -q` prints **only** the numeric ID and suppresses everything else, including the digest column.

But they also want "skip refreshing the index after reset". There's also --hard resets everything, --mixed (default) resets index to HEAD but keeps working directory. Actually git reset --keep <commit> is similar to --hard but safer, keeps changes that are not committed. But the question: "reset head but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command?" Possibly they want `git reset --soft HEAD~1` or `git reset --mixed HEAD~1` (mixed default) which updates index but they want skip refreshing index. There's also `git reset --hard HEAD~1` but that discards changes.

The phrase "skip refreshing the index after reset" suggests using `--soft` which does not touch the index, or using `--merge` maybe? Actually `git reset --merge` is for aborting etc.

Maybe they want `git reset --soft <commit>` to move HEAD, keep index and working tree as is. That keeps local changes (both staged and unstaged). And index is not refreshed.

Alternatively, `git reset --keep <commit>` also preserves changes and skips index refresh? Let's check. The `--keep` option is like `--hard` but attempts to preserve modifications to tracked files and also staged changes. It may update the index? I'm not fully sure.

Better to provide answer: Use `git reset --soft <commit>` to move HEAD while leaving the index and working directory untouched, thus preserving any local changes and not refreshing the index. If you want to reset to a previous commit but keep unstaged changes and avoid updating the index, you can use `git reset --soft HEAD~1` (or the desired commit). If you also want to preserve the staging area as is, `--soft` is the only option that does not touch the index. Alternatively, you can combine with `--mixed` and then `--no-index-refresh`? There's no such option. The default `--mixed` does refresh the index (resets it to the new HEAD). So to skip that, use `--soft`.

Thus answer: `git reset --soft <target>` or `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. Also mention `--keep` as alternative.

Will also explain what each does.

Will provide examples.

Now answer.</think>**Short answer**

```bash
git reset --soft <commit‑or‑ref>
```

- `--soft` moves the `HEAD` reference to the named commit **without touching the index (staging area) or the working‑tree files**.  
- All changes that are already staged **and** all unstaged local modifications stay exactly where they were, so you “keep local changes”.  
- Because the index is left untouched, no “refresh” of the index occurs.

If you want to go back one commit, for example:

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1     # moves HEAD back one commit, keeps everything else
```

---

### Why the other common options don’t meet all three requirements

| Option | Moves HEAD? | Updates the index? | Keeps unstaged changes? |
|--------|-------------|--------------------|------------------------|
| `git reset --hard <commit>` | Yes | **Yes** (index is reset to the new HEAD) | No – working‑tree changes are discarded |
| `git reset --mixed <commit>` (default) | Yes | **Yes** (index is reset to the new HEAD) | Yes – unstaged changes stay in the working tree, but the index **is refreshed** |
| `git reset --soft <commit>` | Yes | **No** (index is left exactly as it was) | Yes – both staged and unstaged changes are preserved |
| `git reset --keep <commit>` | Yes | Mostly left alone, but it may still adjust the index for safety; behaviour is closer to `--hard` when there are conflicts. | Yes, but it can abort if the reset would lose data, so it’s less predictable if you just want “skip refreshing the index”. |

Only `--soft` guarantees that **the index is not refreshed/updated** while still moving `HEAD` and preserving all local modifications.

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| Move HEAD back, keep **all** local changes (staged + unstaged) and **don’t touch the index** | `git reset --soft HEAD~1`  (or `git reset --soft <commit‑hash>`) |
| Move HEAD back, keep **unstaged** changes, **accept that the index will be refreshed** (the default) | `git reset HEAD~1`  (or `git reset --mixed HEAD~1`) |
| Move HEAD back, discard **everything** (including staged & unstaged) | `git reset --hard HEAD~1` |
| Move HEAD back, try to keep changes safe but may still adjust the index | `git reset --keep HEAD~1` (use only when you want a “safe” reset that may refuse if it can’t preserve something) |

---

### TL;DR

- **Use `git reset --soft <ref>`** if you want to reset `HEAD` *and* leave the index exactly as it is, thereby keeping all local changes without any index refresh.  
- All other reset modes either refresh the index (`--mixed`/default) or discard changes (`--hard`).  

That’s the exact combination you asked for: reset HEAD, keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index—all in a single command.

texts:
We need to answer: "What git diff options let me output patch format, and detect copies, in the same command?" The user wants git diff options to output patch format and detect copies. The default git diff already outputs unified diff format (patch format). To detect copies, there is -C option (or --diff-filter? Actually -C detects copies as well as renames). Also -B for deletions, etc. So answer: git diff -C -U... Or git diff --cached? But question: "What git diff options let me output patch format, and detect copies, in the same command?" So we can say: git diff produces patch format by default; to detect copies use -C or --copy. Combined: git diff -C -U3 (or -p). Actually -p shows patch; -C enables copy detection. Also --stat, --numstat, etc. Provide command: git diff -C -p <tree-ish> <path>. Or git diff --no-index? But answer: Use git diff -C -p or git diff --patch -C.

We can also mention -M for rename detection, -C includes both copies and renames. Also -S for content search.

Thus answer: Use git diff -C -p (or -U N). Provide explanation. Might also mention that you can combine with --no-index for file differences.

We'll answer accordingly.</think>**Short answer**

```bash
git diff -C -p   # (or equivalently `git diff --patch -C`)
```

- **`-p`** (or simply running `git diff` without any extra formatting) produces the **unified‑diff “patch” format** that shows the actual line‑by‑line changes.
- **`-C`** tells Git to **detect copies as well as renames** (it also implies rename detection `-M`).  
  When a piece of code appears unchanged in another file, Git will report it as a *copy* with the `copy from`/`copy to` lines in the patch.

You can also tweak the diff’s context/lines with `-U<N>` (e.g., `-U3` shows three lines of context around each change) while keeping the patch format and copy detection:

```bash
git diff -C -U3   # patch with three lines of context + copy detection
```

---

### Why this works

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| **`git diff`** (no options) | By default outputs a **unified diff** (the classic patch format). |
| **`-p`** | Synonym for the default patch output; explicit if you want to be clear. |
| **`-C`** | Enables **copy detection** (and, by default, rename detection `-M`). If a chunk of text is found unchanged in another file, the patch will contain lines like `copy from ` / `copy to `. |
| **`-M`** | (implicit with `-C`) Detects **renames**. |
| **`-B`** | (optional) Ignore changes that are just blank‑line changes. |
| **`-U<N>`** | Controls how many lines of context are shown around each hunk (useful when you want a bit more surrounding text). |
| **`--stat` / `--numstat`** | Show file‑level statistics; not needed for a pure patch. |

---

### Common practical forms

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **Basic patch + copy detection** | `git diff -C -p` |
| **Patch with context lines + copy detection** | `git diff -C -U3 -p` |
| **Only show copies (no renames)** | `git diff -C -p --no-renames` (rarely needed; `-C` already includes renames) |
| **Combine with other filters** (e.g., ignore whitespace) | `git diff -C -w -p` ( `-w` ignores whitespace changes) |

---

### Quick test

```bash
# Create a temporary repo to see the effect
mkdir /tmp/testdiff && cd /tmp/testdiff
git init
echo "line1" > a.txt
echo "line1" > b.txt   # same content, different file
git add .
git commit -m "initial"

# Make a change that copies content from a.txt into b.txt
echo "line2" >> b.txt

# Show diff with copy detection
git diff -C -p
```

You’ll see something like:

```
diff --git a/b.txt b/b.txt
index ... -> ...
--- a/b.txt
+++ b.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 line1
+line2
 copy from a.txt
```

The `copy from a.txt` line appears because of the `-C` flag, while the rest of the output is the usual unified‑diff patch.

---

**TL;DR:** Use `git diff -C -p` (or `git diff --patch -C`) to get a patch‑format diff that also flags copies. Add `-U<N>` for more context if desired.

JOURNALCTL(1)                                journalctl                               JOURNALCTL(1)

NAME
       journalctl - Print log entries from the systemd journal

SYNOPSIS

       journalctl [OPTIONS...] [MATCHES...]

DESCRIPTION
       journalctl is used to print the log entries stored in the journal by systemd-
       journald.service(8) and systemd-journal-remote.service(8).

       If called without parameters, it will show the contents of the journal accessible to the
       calling user, starting with the oldest entry collected.

       If one or more match arguments are passed, the output is filtered accordingly. A match is in
       the format "FIELD=VALUE", e.g.  "_SYSTEMD_UNIT=httpd.service", referring to the components
       of a structured journal entry. See systemd.journal-fields(7) for a list of well-known
       fields. If multiple matches are specified matching different fields, the log entries are
       filtered by both, i.e. the resulting output will show only entries matching all the
       specified matches of this kind. If two matches apply to the same field, then they are
       automatically matched as alternatives, i.e. the resulting output will show entries matching
       any of the specified matches for the same field. Finally, the character "+" may appear as a
       separate word between other terms on the command line. This causes all matches before and
       after to be combined in a disjunction (i.e. logical OR).

       It is also possible to filter the entries by specifying an absolute file path as an
       argument. The file path may be a file or a symbolic link and the file must exist at the time
       of the query. If a file path refers to an executable binary, an "_EXE=" match for the

messages.content: With git diff, how do I detect renames, and also show diffstat instead of patch?

texts:
User asks: "With git diff, how do I detect renames, and also show diffstat instead of patch?" They want to know git diff options to detect renames and show diffstat instead of patch.

We can answer: git diff -M (or --detect-renames) to detect renames; also -S for content, -C for copies; and --stat to show diffstat, and --numstat for more detailed, or --dirstat. Also can combine: git diff -M --stat. Or git diff --stat -M. Also can use -p to get patch; but they want diffstat instead of patch. So use --stat.

Thus answer: Use git diff -M --stat (or git diff --detect-renames --stat). Also can use -C --stat for copies. Also can use --numstat for per-file additions/deletions.

We can also show example commands.

We may also check git help via bash if needed, but we can answer from knowledge.

Thus final answer.</think>**Short answer**

```bash
# Detect renames and show a diffstat (file‑level summary) instead of the full patch
git diff -M --stat
```

or, equivalently (the “‑‑detect‑renames” long form):

```bash
git diff --detect-renames --stat
```

---

### What the options do

| Option | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **`-M`** (or **`--detect-renames`**) | Tells Git to detect *renames* (and *copies* if you also use `-C`). Without it, a renamed file looks like a deletion + addition. |
| **`--stat`** | Prints a **diffstat** at the bottom of the output – a one‑line summary for each path showing the number of added and deleted lines, plus the total number of files changed. It suppresses the patch body (`-p`). |
| **`-C`** | In addition to renames, also detects *copies*. Use `git diff -C --stat` if you want copy detection as well. |
| **`--numstat`** | Like `--stat` but shows the *exact* addition/deletion counts for each file (e.g., ` 12  34 file.py`). Useful when you need the numbers themselves, not just the bar‑graph. |
| **`--dirstat`** | Shows a breakdown of the changes by directory (percentage of total lines changed per directory). |

---

### Common useful variants

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **Basic rename detection + diffstat** | `git diff -M --stat` |
| **Detect renames *and* copies** | `git diff -C --stat` |
| **Show exact addition/deletion counts** | `git diff --numstat` |
| **Show per‑directory statistics** | `git diff --dirstat` |
| **Combine rename detection with a summary that still includes the patch header (but not the full diff)** | `git diff -M --stat -p`  (the `-p` still prints the patch, but the `--stat` part adds the summary; you can omit `-p` if you only want the stat) |
| **Limit the diff to a specific path or glob** | `git diff -M --stat -- path/to/stuff` |

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

```bash
# Rename detection + diffstat (no patch)
git diff -M --stat

# Rename + copy detection + diffstat
git diff -C --stat

# Exact addition/deletion numbers per file
git diff --numstat

# Per‑directory stats
git diff --dirstat
```

---

### How it looks in practice

```text
$ git diff -M --stat
 README.md |  5 ++++-
 src/main.c | 12 +----------
 2 files changed, 6 insertions(+), 11 deletions(-)
```

The last line (`2 files changed, 6 insertions(+), 11 deletions(-)`) is the **diffstat** summary. If you omit `-M`, a renamed file would appear as:

```text
--- a/oldname.txt
+++ /dev/null
@@ -1 +0,0 @@
...
--- /dev/null
+++ b/newname.txt
@@ -0,0 +1 @@
...
```

So `-M` makes Git recognise that `oldname.txt` → `newname.txt` is a rename and collapse the two `--- / +++` blocks into a single entry in the stat.

---

**TL;DR:**  
`git diff -M --stat` (or `git diff --detect-renames --stat`) will show you a diffstat while also telling Git to treat renames as renames instead of delete‑plus‑add. Adjust with `-C` for copies, `--numstat` for raw numbers, or `--dirstat` for directory‑level breakdowns.

Let's respond.</think>Git itself doesn’t have a “‑U” flag on `git commit`, but you control the amount of context that appears in the diffs that Git shows (or that you export) with the **‑U <n>** option of the diff‑related commands.

### 1. Show <n> lines of context in a `git diff`

```bash
git diff -U<n>
```

- `‑U<n>` (or **‑u<n>**) tells Git to include *<n>* lines of context around each hunk of changes.
- If you omit the flag, Git uses the default (usually 3 lines).

Example – 5 lines of context:

```bash
git diff -U5
```

### 2. Export a patch with context for use with `git commit`

If you want to create a patch file that contains the context and then apply it (and commit) later:

```bash
# Generate a patch with <n> context lines
git diff -U<n> > my‑patch.patch

# Inspect the patch
head -n 30 my‑patch.patch   # shows the first hunks with context

# Apply the patch (this stages the changes)
git apply my‑patch.patch

# Commit the applied changes
git commit -m "Your commit message"
```

### 3. Use it with `git format‑patch` (for series of commits)

```bash
git format-patch -U<n> <range>
```

- This generates `.patch` files for the specified range of commits, each containing <n> lines of context.
- You can then edit or send the patches; when applied with `git am` or `git apply`, the context is preserved.

### 4. Quick “one‑liner” to commit while seeing the diff

If you just want to see a diff with extra context *while* you’re about to commit, you can view it with `‑U<n>` and then commit as usual:

```bash
# Show the diff with 7 lines of context
git diff -U7

# When you’re ready, commit (the diff you just saw won’t be part of the commit,
# it’s only for your inspection)
git commit -m "Your commit message"
```

### Summary

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| Show *n* context lines in the current working‑tree diff | `git diff -U<n>` |
| Export a patch with *n* context lines to later `git apply` + `git commit` | `git diff -U<n> > patch.txt` → `git apply patch.txt` → `git commit` |
| Generate a patch series (e.g., for `git send‑mail` or `git am`) with context | `git format-patch -U<n> <commit‑range>` |
| View a diff with context before you commit (informational only) | `git diff -U<n>` then `git commit` |

So the key is the **‑U <n>** flag on any `git diff`‑family command. Once you have the diff you want, you can stage and commit the changes normally.

texts:
The user asks: "How do I edit the todo list during an interactive rebase using git rebase?" They want instructions on editing the todo list during an interactive rebase. I should provide explanation: use `git rebase -i HEAD~N`, then change pick to edit, etc. Also can use `git rebase -i` to open editor, modify lines, save, quit. Then git will pause at each 'edit' command, allowing you to amend, reorder, squash, etc. Also can use `git rebase --continue` after editing. Provide steps.

I should maybe demonstrate with a quick command to open the todo list, maybe show sample content. Could also show how to use `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR` to automate, but main answer is interactive.

No need for tools. Just answer.</think>When you start an **interactive rebase** Git opens a file (the “todo list”) that describes which operations Git will perform and in what order.  
The most common way to edit that list is:

1. **Start the rebase** – pick the number of commits you want to touch.  
2. **Change `pick` to `edit`** (or `e`) for any commit you want to pause on.  
3. **Save & close** the file.  
4. Git will stop at each commit marked `edit`, letting you modify the commit (amend, change the message, reorder, squash, etc.).  
5. When you’re done, **continue** the rebase.

Below is a step‑by‑step example and a few tips/tricks.

---

## 1️⃣ Start the interactive rebase

```bash
# Edit the last 5 commits (you can use any ref, e.g. HEAD~3, a branch name, etc.)
git rebase -i HEAD~5
```

Git will fire up your default editor with a file that looks like this:

```
pick 1a2b3c4 Commit 5
pick 2d3e4f5 Commit 4
pick 3g5h6i7 Commit 3
pick 4j7k8l9 Commit 2
pick 5m9n0o1 Commit 1
```

*(Newer Git versions may also add comments explaining the available commands.)*

---

## 2️⃣ Mark the commits you want to edit

Change the word `pick` to `edit` (or the short form `e`) next to the commit(s) you want Git to stop on.

**Example – edit the 3rd and 5th commits:**

```
pick 1a2b3c4 Commit 5
pick 2d3e4f5 Commit 4
edit 3g5h6i7 Commit 3   # <-- changed from `pick` to `edit`
pick 4j7k8l9 Commit 2
edit 5m9n0o1 Commit 1   # <-- changed from `pick` to `edit`
```

Save the file and quit the editor (usually `:wq` in Vi/Vim, `Ctrl‑X` → `Y` in Nano, or ⌘‑S / ⌘‑Q in GUI editors).

---

## 3️⃣ Git pauses at each `edit` marker

You’ll see something like:

```
Stopped at 3g5h6i7... Commit 3
You are currently editing commit 3g5h6i7.
```

At this point you can do whatever you need:

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **Change the commit message** | `git commit --amend` (edit the message, then save & quit) |
| **Add or change files, then amend** | `git add <files>` → `git commit --amend` |
| **Squash the current commit into the previous one** | `git reset HEAD~1` (undo the edit marker) → re‑run the rebase with `pick` for the squashed commit, or use `git merge --squash` followed by `git commit --amend` |
| **Reorder commits** | After you’re done with one `edit`, you can re‑run the rebase with a different order (see the “reordering” section below). |
| **Drop a commit** | `git reset HEAD~1` and then `git rebase --continue` (or just `git reset --soft HEAD~1` and `git reset HEAD` if you want to remove it entirely). |

When you’re satisfied with the commit, **continue the rebase**:

```bash
git rebase --continue
```

Git will automatically move to the next `edit` (or finish the rebase if there are no more).

---

## 4️⃣ Reordering commits (without editing each one)

If you only want to change the *order* of the commits, you can re‑arrange the lines in the todo list **before** saving:

```
pick 1a2b3c4 Commit 5          # will be 1st after rebase
pick 2d3e4f5 Commit 4          # will be 2nd
edit 3g5h6i7 Commit 3   <-- move up
pick 4j7k8l9 Commit 2   <-- move down
edit 5m9n0o1 Commit 1   <-- move to bottom
```

After saving, Git will apply the commits in the new order, stopping only where you put `edit`.

---

## 5️⃣ Using a custom editor ( `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR` )

If you prefer a different editor or want to automate a sed‑style change, set the `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR` variable:

```bash
# Open the todo list in nano and allow inline editing
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR="nano -w" git rebase -i HEAD~5
```

Or, to replace every `pick` with `edit` automatically (not recommended for production, but handy for demos):

```bash
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR="sed -i 's/^pick /edit /'" git rebase -i HEAD~5
```

---

## 6️⃣ Common patterns

| Desired outcome | Todo‑list changes |
|-----------------|-------------------|
| **Amend commit message only** | `edit <commit>` → `git commit --amend` → `git rebase --continue` |
| **Squash a commit into the previous one** | `pick <commit>` → after `edit`, run `git reset HEAD~1` (undo the edit) → change the upper commit to `edit` → `git commit --amend` (will include the lower commit) → `git rebase --continue` |
| **Drop a commit** | `drop <commit>` (or change `pick` to `drop`) |
| **Rename a commit** | `edit <commit>` → `git commit --amend -m "new message"` → `git rebase --continue` |

       configuration file. (See git-config(1)).

           .git/FETCH_HEAD. Without this option old data in .git/FETCH_HEAD will be overwritten.

User asks: "What docker images options let me only show image ids, and show digests, in the same command?" They want to know Docker `docker images` options to show only image IDs and also show digests. We need to provide command(s). Likely `docker images --format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"` or using `--filter` maybe. The default `docker images` shows REPOSITORY, TAG, IMAGE ID, CREATED, SIZE. To show digest, need to use `docker images --digests` flag, which adds a DIGEST column. To show only image IDs and digests, we can combine `--format` with placeholders: `docker images --format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"`. Also `--digests` alone adds digest column but also shows other columns. To show only ID and digest, use format.

Thus answer: use `docker images --digests --format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"`. Or just `docker images --format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"` maybe without `--digests` but digest may be empty unless images have digest (for images built with BuildKit, etc). The `--digests` flag ensures digest is shown.

Thus respond with command and explanation.</think>You can combine the **`--digests`** flag (which adds a `DIGEST` column) with the **`--format`** flag (which lets you pick exactly which fields you want to see).

### One‑liner that shows only the image ID and its digest

```bash
docker images --digests --format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"
```

**What it does**

| Option | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `--digests` | Instructs Docker to compute and display the image digest (the SHA‑256 hash) for each image. Without this flag the digest column is omitted (or empty). |
| `--format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"` | Uses Go’s template syntax to output **only** the `ID` and `Digest` fields, separated by a space. You can adjust the separator or add other placeholders if you need extra info. |

### If you just want the default output with the digest column

```bash
docker images --digests
```

That command prints the usual table (REPOSITORY, TAG, IMAGE ID, CREATED, SIZE) **plus** a `DIGEST` column on the far right.

### Quick reference of useful placeholders for `--format`

| Placeholder | Meaning |
|-------------|---------|
| `{{.ID}}` | Image ID (short form) |
| `{{.Repository}}` | Repository name |
| `{{.Tag}}` | Tag |
| `{{.Digest}}` | Image digest (only shown when `--digests` is used) |
| `{{.CreatedAt}}` | Creation timestamp |
| `{{.Size}}` | Image size |

You can mix and match them, e.g.:

```bash
docker images --digests --format "{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} -> {{.ID}} ({{.Digest}})"
```

That would give you a concise line‑by‑line list like:

```
nginx:latest -> 5f1a2b3c (sha256:abcdef123456...)
```

We need to answer: What journalctl options let me print the cursor after all the entries, and ellipsize fields, in the same command?

From help: `--show-cursor` prints the cursor after all the entries. `--no-full` ellipsizes fields. So the command can combine both: `journalctl --show-cursor --no-full`. Also possibly `-o` but those are the two options.

Thus answer: use `--show-cursor` and `--no-full`. Provide example.

</think>Both of those behaviours are controlled by separate `journalctl` options:

| Goal | Option | What it does |
|------|--------|--------------|
| **Print the cursor after all entries** | **`--show-cursor`** | After the list of log lines is printed, the cursor that marks the last shown entry is emitted on stderr (or stdout, depending on the pager). |
| **Ellipsize (truncate) long fields** | **`--no-full`** | Instead of showing the complete field values, `journalctl` cuts them off with “...” so the output stays compact. |

You can use them together in a single command, e.g.:

```bash
journalctl --show-cursor --no-full
```

*Example output (truncated fields, cursor at the end)*  

```
-- Journal begins at Tue 2023‑01‑01 00:00:00 UTC, ends at Tue 2023‑01‑02 23:59:59 UTC --
Jan 01 12:34:56 host service[1234]: some log message that gets ellip...
Jan 01 12:35:01 host service[1235]: another message...
... <cursor>=0xabcdef1234567890
```

The cursor line (`... <cursor>=0x...`) appears after all the entries, and each field that would otherwise be very long is shortened with “...”.

messages.content: What git reset options let me reset head but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command?

texts:
We need to answer: "What git reset options let me reset head but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command?" The user wants git reset options that reset HEAD but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command.

We need to provide the options: git reset --soft <commit> moves HEAD to commit, keeps index and working directory changes. But they want keep local changes and skip refreshing the index after reset. Actually git reset without --hard resets HEAD to specified commit, but by default it resets the index to match the new HEAD, but keeps working directory changes. However they want to skip refreshing the index after reset, i.e., not update the index. That's done with --soft? Actually --soft moves HEAD and keeps index and working tree as is. That means local changes remain staged? Let's recall:

- git reset --soft <commit>: moves HEAD to <commit>, does NOT touch the index file or the working directory (any changes remain staged as they were). So local changes are kept, index unchanged.

- git reset --mixed <commit> (default): moves HEAD, resets the index to match the new HEAD, but keeps working directory files. So changes become unstaged.

- git reset --hard <commit>: resets everything including working directory.

If they want to reset HEAD but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command. That sounds like git reset --soft <commit>. Because that keeps index unchanged and keeps working directory changes.

But maybe they want to reset HEAD to a previous commit, keep the changes in the working directory, and not update the index (i.e., keep index as is). That's exactly --soft.

Alternatively, they might want to use git reset HEAD~1 --soft. Or maybe they want to use git reset --soft HEAD~1.

Thus answer: use `git reset --soft <commit>` or `git reset --soft HEAD~N`. Explanation.

We can also mention that you can combine with `--merge` or `--keep` for more complex scenarios, but the direct answer is `--soft`.

Thus respond with explanation and example command.

Check if any nuance: "skip refreshing the index after reset". The default reset --mixed refreshes the index. So to skip that, use --soft.

Thus answer.</think>**Short answer**

```bash
git reset --soft <commit>
```

(or `git reset --soft HEAD~N` to go N commits back).

---

### What it does

| Option | Moves `HEAD` | Updates the **index** (staging area) | Updates the **working directory** |
|--------|--------------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `--soft` | ✅ yes | **no** – the index stays exactly as it was | **no** – all files you had remain in the working tree, unchanged |
| `--mixed` (default) | ✅ yes | **yes** – the index is reset to match the new `HEAD`; any changes become *unstaged* | **yes** – working‑tree files are kept, but they’re now unstaged |
| `--hard` | ✅ yes | **yes** | **yes** – working‑tree is also thrown away |

`--soft` is the only built‑in reset mode that **keeps the index untouched** while still moving `HEAD` to the requested commit. Consequently, any changes you had (staged or unstaged) stay exactly where they were, and the index is *not* refreshed/updated.

### Typical usage

```bash
# Go back 3 commits, keep everything exactly as it is now
git reset --soft HEAD~3
```

or, targeting a specific hash:

```bash
git reset --soft abc1234
```

After running that command:

* `HEAD` now points to the chosen commit.
* The index (staging area) still reflects whatever was staged **before** the reset.
* Your working‑directory files are unchanged – they still contain the content you had before the reset.

### Why the other options won’t meet the requirement

* **`git reset` (or `--mixed`)** – after the command the index is reset to the new `HEAD`; any previously‑staged changes become unstaged. This *does* refresh the index, which you said you want to avoid.
* **`git reset --hard`** – blows away both the index and the working directory, so local changes are lost.
* **`git checkout` / `git restore`** – those commands are for switching branches or restoring files, not for moving `HEAD` while preserving the index.

---

### TL;DR

- To **reset HEAD** and **keep local changes** **without touching the index**, use **`--soft`**.
- Example: `git reset --soft HEAD~1` (or `git reset --soft <commit‑hash>`).

We'll answer accordingly.</think>**Short answer**

```bash
git diff -p -C   # (or `git diff --patch --copy`)
```

* `-p` — output the changes in **patch/ unified‑diff** format (the same format you’d see with `git show` or a `git diff` that hasn’t been suppressed).  
* `-C` — **detect copies** as well as renames.  When a file that appears in the “after” state already exists elsewhere in the tree (and its content is the same), Git will emit a `copy from <commit>:<path>` line in the patch instead of a new‑file insertion.

You can add other common flags on the same command line, e.g.:

```bash
git diff -p -C --stat      # show a summary line after the patch
git diff -p -C --no-index  # compare two arbitrary files on disk
git diff -p -C --find-copies-harder   # also compare files that haven’t been modified
```

**Explanation of the flags**

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `-p`, `--patch` | Generate a patch (unified diff) that includes the `---`/`+++` lines, context, and hunks. |
| `-C`, `--copy` | In addition to detecting renames, Git looks for files that are **copies** of existing files elsewhere in the comparison set. The patch will contain a `copy from <source>` line when a file is identified as a copy. |
| `-M`, `--rename` | (often used together with `-C`) detect renames. `-C` alone already implies rename detection, but you can be explicit with `-C -M` if you want both explicitly. |
| `--find-copies-harder` | After the fast‑path copy detection, Git will also scan files that *haven’t* been modified to see if they match any added/removed file. This makes copy detection more thorough but is slower. |
| `--stat` | (optional) Print a terse summary of changed files, insertions/deletions after the patch. |

**Typical one‑liner**

```bash
git diff -p -C          # patch format + copy detection
```

or, if you want the extra thoroughness:

```bash
git diff -p -C --find-copies-harder
```

Both commands will emit a unified diff *and* any `copy from …` annotations that Git can find, all in a single invocation.

Thus answer: use `docker images --format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"`. If you want only image IDs and digests, maybe also exclude tag: use `docker images --format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"`. Could also use `docker images -q` to show only IDs, but not digests. To show both, use format.

</think>You can use the `docker images` format flag to pick exactly the fields you want.  
The built‑in template variables you need are:

* `{{.ID}}` – the full image ID (use `--no-trunc` to get the 64‑character ID instead of the short form)  
* `{{.Digest}}` – the image digest (e.g. `sha256:…`). Digests are only shown for immutable tags, but the format will print an empty string if there’s no digest.

### One‑liner

```bash
docker images --no-trunc --format "{{.ID}} {{.Digest}}"
```

* `--no-trunc` – ensures the full image ID is displayed (otherwise Docker truncates it to the first 12 characters).  
* `--format` – lets you specify a Go template; the string above prints the ID, a space, then the digest on the same line.

### Example output

```
abc123def456... sha256:3a7d5c9e8f...
```

If you prefer a table‑style output with a header, you can add the header text directly in the format string:

```bash
docker images --no-trunc --format "IMAGE ID\tDIGEST\n{{.ID}}\t{{.Digest}}"
```

That command will show **only** the image ID and its digest, without the usual `REPOSITORY`, `TAG`, `CREATED`, `SIZE` columns.

| Goal | journalctl command | How it works |
|------|-------------------|--------------|
| **View the built‑in “explanation” that systemd attaches to a unit** | `journalctl -u <unit‑name>` | If the service unit file contains a `Description=` line, journalctl prints it as part of the message. |
| **Add your own explanatory note that later shows up in `journalctl`** | `systemd‑cat -t <tag> "your note"`  **or** `logger -t <tag> "your note"` | The tag (`<tag>`) becomes a `SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER` field. You can then pull just those entries with `journalctl -t <tag>`. |

| **Filter journal entries that have an explanation (non‑empty `MESSAGE`)** | `journalctl -o short‑precise | grep -v '^$'` | Anything that is not an empty line is a message that journalctl can display. |

Below is a step‑by‑step guide that covers the most common ways to **add** message explanations and then **retrieve** them with `journalctl`.

---

## 1. What “message explanation” means in the journal

Systemd stores two text fields for every log entry:

| Field | Where it comes from | What you usually see |
|-------|--------------------|----------------------|
| **`MESSAGE`** | The actual text you write (via `logger`, `systemd‑cat`, a service’s `stdout`/`stderr`, etc.) | The big line you see with `journalctl -u foo`. |
| **`Description`** (optional) | The `Description=` line in the unit file (or the `Description` key in a `.service` drop‑in) | Shown by `systemctl status <unit>` and also appears as part of the `MESSAGE` when you use `journalctl -u <unit>`. |

If a unit has a `Description`, journalctl will automatically include it when you list the unit’s logs:

```bash
$ journalctl -u my‑service.service
-- Logs for my‑service.service ---
Jan 12 10:13:45 hostname systemd[1]: Started my‑service.service.
Jan 12 10:13:46 hostname my‑service[1234]: My custom explanation goes here.
```

So **“adding a message explanation where available”** usually means one of two things:

1. **Add a `Description=` to a systemd unit file** – then `journalctl -u <unit>` will show it automatically.
2. **Inject your own free‑form text** via `systemd‑cat`/`logger` – then you can filter/retrive it with `journalctl -t <tag>`.

---

## 2. Add a `Description=` to a service unit (the “native” way)

1. **Locate (or create) the unit file**  

   ```bash
   $ systemctl edit --full my‑service.service   # opens the file in $EDITOR
   ```

2. **Add or edit the `Description` line**  

   ```ini
   [Unit]
   Description=My custom explanation of what this service does
               and why it may emit the messages you see.
   ```

   *You can use multiple lines; just keep the indentation consistent.*

3. **Reload systemd and re‑query the journal**  

   ```bash
   $ systemctl daemon-reload
   $ journalctl -u my‑service.service
   ```

   The `Description` appears at the top of the log (or alongside the first message), exactly what most users mean by “explanation where available”.

---

## 3. Inject your own explanatory text at runtime

If you can’t (or don’t want to) modify a unit file, you can still push a custom message into the journal. The two most common helpers are **`systemd‑cat`** and **`logger`**.

### 3.1 Using `systemd‑cat`

```bash
# Write a tagged message that journalctl can later filter
systemd-cat -t my‑explanation "This is the explanation the admin added."
```

* `-t <tag>` sets the `SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER` field.  
* The message ends up in the journal with a tag you can later select.

Thus final answer.</think>Git provides the **`-U <n>`** (or **`--unified=<n>`**) option for the `git commit` command.  
It controls how many lines of context are shown in the diff that Git records for the commit.

```bash
# Show 5 lines of context around each change
git commit -U5
```

or, using the long form:

```bash
git commit --unified=5
```

### What it does
- `-U<n>` (unified context) tells Git to include **`<n>` lines of context** before and after every hunk of diff output that is stored in the commit’s underlying tree.
- If you omit the number, Git falls back to the `diff.context` configuration value; if that is also unset, the default is **3 lines**.

### Example
```bash
# Commit all changes with 7 lines of context per diff
git commit -U7 -m "Add feature X with full context"
```

### Permanent default (optional)
You can also set the number permanently in your Git configuration so you don’t have to type it each time:

```bash
git config --global diff.context 7   # 7 lines of context for all diffs
```

After setting `diff.context`, you can simply run `git commit` without `-U` and the specified context will be used.

### Related option
If you also want context **between** diff hunks (which can merge nearby hunks together), use:

```bash
git commit --inter-hunk-context=<n>
```

---

**Summary**

| Flag                     | Meaning                              |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `-U<n>` / `--unified=n`  | `n` lines of context around each hunk |
| `--inter-hunk-context=n`| `n` lines of context between hunks   |
| `git config diff.context n` | permanent default for all diffs   |

Just prepend `-U<n>` (or `--unified=n`) to your `git commit` command, and the diff recorded in the commit will contain the requested amount of context.

       the current user is used to find the key for signing. The configuration variable gpg.program
       is used to specify a custom signing binary.

       creation date, the tagger name and e-mail, a tagging message, and an optional cryptographic

       object).

texts:
The user asks: "How do I edit the todo list during an interactive rebase using git rebase?" We need to explain how to edit the todo list during an interactive rebase. Provide steps: `git rebase -i HEAD~N`, change pick to edit, etc. Also mention using `git rebase --editor` to edit the file, changing commands (pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop). After saving, git will pause at the command with 'edit', where you can amend, modify, then continue with `git rebase --continue`. Also talk about using `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR` to automate, or using `git rebase -i` with a script.

We should maybe provide examples.

We can also optionally show how to open the editor, modify lines, save and quit.

Thus answer.

No tool needed.

Proceed to final.</think>Editing the todo list of an interactive rebase is a quick way to change how Git processes a series of commits (pick, reword, squash, edit, drop, etc.). Here’s the step‑by‑step workflow:

---

## 1️⃣ Start the interactive rebase

```bash
# Edit the last N commits (replace N with the number you want)
git rebase -i HEAD~N
```

*or* rebase onto another branch:

```bash
git rebase -i <base-branch>
```

Git will open a text file (the **todo list**) that looks like:

```
pick 1111111 Commit 1
pick 2222222 Commit 2
pick 3333333 Commit 3
pick 4444444 Commit 4
pick 5555555 Commit 5
```

---

## 2️⃣ Edit the file

Open the file in your default editor and change any line’s command:

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `pick`  | Use the commit as‑is (default). |
| `reword`| Edit the commit message after the commit is picked. |
| `edit`| Pause the rebase so you can modify the commit (add/change files, amend, etc.). |
| `squash`| Merge the commit into the previous one **and** prompt for a combined message. |
| `fixup`| Merge the commit into the previous one **without** prompting for a message (the previous commit’s message is kept). |
| `drop`  | Delete the commit entirely. |

**Typical changes**

- **Drop a commit**: just delete its line.
- **Squash two commits**: change the second line from `pick` to `squash`.
- **Edit a commit** (e.g., to fix a typo or add a forgotten file): change its line to `edit`.

Example after editing (now the second commit will be squashed into the first, and the fifth commit will be dropped):

```
pick 1111111 Commit 1
squash 2222222 Commit 2   # will be merged with #1
pick 3333333 Commit 3
pick 4444444 Commit 4
drop 5555555 Commit 5    # will be removed
```

Save and quit the editor. Git will then apply the commands in order.

---

## 3️⃣ What happens when a command is `edit`

If you change a line to `edit`, Git will:

1. **Pause** the rebase right after that commit is checked out.
2. Give you a shell prompt where you can run any Git commands you need (`git status`, `git add`, `git commit --amend`, etc.).
3. After you’re satisfied, run:

```bash
git rebase --continue
```

Git will then apply the remaining commits in the list.

---

## 4️⃣ Common post‑edit actions

| Goal | Command(s) |
|------|------------|
| **Amend the just‑edited commit** (e.g., change its message or add files) | ```bash git commit --amend   # edit message & files, then save ``` |
| **Add a forgotten file** | ```bash git add <file>   # then ``` |
| **Change the commit message** (when the todo line was `reword`) | Git will open a second editor for just that commit message after the rebase pauses. |
| **Finish the rebase** after you’ve made your changes | ```bash git rebase --continue ``` |
| **Abort the whole rebase** and go back to the original state | ```bash git rebase --abort ``` |

---

## 5️⃣ Automating or scripting the todo list

If you frequently want the same modifications, you can supply a custom **sequence editor**:

```bash
# Example: a shell script that replaces 'pick' with 'edit' for the 3rd commit
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR="sed -i '3s/^pick/edit/' \"$1\"" git rebase -i HEAD~4
```

Or you can generate the todo file yourself and pipe it:

```bash
# Create a custom todo file
cat > /tmp/rebase-todo <<'EOF'
pick 1111111 Commit 1
edit 2222222 Commit 2   # we want to edit this one
pick 3333333 Commit 3
EOF

# Use the file directly (requires Git ≥2.36 with `--todo-file`):
git rebase -i --todo-file=/tmp/rebase-todo HEAD~3
```

---

## 6️⃣ Quick cheat‑sheet

| Action | Todo‑list change |
|--------|------------------|
| Keep as‑is | `pick <hash> <msg>` |
| Edit commit message later | `reword <hash> <msg>` |
| Pause to modify the commit (add/amend) | `edit <hash> <msg>` |
| Merge into previous & keep its message | `fixup <hash> <msg>` |
| Merge into previous & prompt for a new combined message | `squash <hash> <msg>` |
| Remove the commit entirely | `drop <hash> <msg>` |

---

### TL;DR

1. `git rebase -i HEAD~N`  
2. Open the editor, change `pick` → `edit` (or `squash`, `drop`, etc.)  
3. Save & quit → Git processes up to the `edit` command, then stops.  
4. Make your changes, `git add`/`git commit --amend` as needed, then `git rebase --continue`.  

That’s all you need to edit the todo list during an interactive rebase!

       want to "catch up" to the work done on the master branch.

`--quit` ends the rebase run and leaves **HEAD exactly where it is** – at the last commit that was successfully applied during the rebase. The branch is then back to a clean, non‑rebase state, but the commit you ended up with stays as the tip of the branch.

---

### Why `--quit` instead of `--abort`?

| Command | What it does to HEAD | When you’d use it |
|---------|----------------------|-------------------|
| `git rebase --abort` | **Resets** HEAD to the commit it had **before** the rebase started (i.e. undoes everything the rebase did). | You want to completely throw the rebase away and go back to where you were before you typed `git rebase`. |
| `git rebase --quit` | **Leaves** HEAD at the **last successfully replayed commit** (the result of the rebase). The rebase is terminated, but the new history stays. | You want to stop the rebase *and* keep the work that was already applied. |
| `git rebase --skip` | Skips the current commit and continues the rebase. | You want to discard a single problematic commit and keep going. |
| `git rebase --continue` | Finishes the rebase after you’ve resolved a conflict. | Normal flow when the rebase is paused for conflicts. |

---

### Step‑by‑step example

1. **Start a rebase** (interactive or automatic)  

   ```bash
   git rebase -i main   # or just `git rebase main`
   ```

2. **At some point** you decide you want to stop, but you like the commits you’ve already got.

3. **Quit the rebase, keeping the current HEAD**:

   ```bash
   git rebase --quit
   ```

   - Git finishes the in‑progress rebase, stops the “rebase in‑memory” stack, and points HEAD at the tip of the newly‑rebased series.
   - Your branch is now on the new commit tree, and you can carry on with normal `git` operations (push, merge, etc.).

4. **If you later realize you wanted to throw everything away**, you can always run:

   ```bash
   git rebase --abort   # returns HEAD to the pre‑rebase state
   ```

---

### Quick cheat‑sheet

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| Undo everything, go back to where you were before the rebase | `git rebase --abort` |
| Stop the rebase **and** keep the commits you’ve already applied | `git rebase --quit` |
| Skip a single commit that’s causing trouble (and continue) | `git rebase --skip` |
| Resolve a conflict and finish the rebase | `git rebase --continue` |

---

**TL;DR:** If you want to “abort” a rebase *but* keep HEAD where it currently is (at the last applied commit), run `git rebase --quit`.

texts:
We need to answer: "What git diff options let me output patch format, and detect copies, in the same command?" The user asks for git diff options to output patch format and detect copies, in same command.

We need to provide the relevant git diff flags: -p (patch), --diff-filter? Actually to detect copies there is -C option, or --copies. git diff -p -C maybe. Also -R? Actually -C detects copies as well as renames. There's also --find-copies-harder. So command: git diff -p -C --find-copies-harder. Or git diff -p -C -B maybe.

Thus answer: use git diff with -p (patch output) and -C (copy detection). Possibly also --stat? but they'll just want patch format and copy detection. Provide example: git diff -p -C. Also mention -C implies copy detection, and can add --find-copies-harder for more thorough.

Thus answer.</think>**Git diff command that gives you a patch‑format output **and** detects copies in a single run**

```sh
git diff -p -C
```

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| **`-p`** | *Patch output* – shows the diff in the unified‑diff format (the same format you’d see with `git show` or a regular `git diff` without any special formatting). |
| **`-C`** | *Copy detection* – tells `git diff` to detect files that have been **copied** (as well as renamed). If a file’s content appears unchanged elsewhere in the tree, the diff will list it as a copy (`copy from …` / `copy to …`). |

### Common variations

| Variation | Effect |
|-----------|--------|
| `git diff -p -C --find-copies-harder` | In addition to simple copies, runs a more thorough content‑matching pass (useful when copies are partial or heavily modified). |
| `git diff -p -C -B` | Also detects **renames** (`-B` = “allow deletion + creation” → rename detection). Combined with `-C` you get both renames *and* copies. |
| `git diff --no-index -p -C <file1> <file2>` | Useful for comparing two arbitrary files that aren’t necessarily tracked by Git; still gives patch output and copy‑detection logic (though copy detection is less meaningful when comparing just two files). |

### Quick example

```sh
# Show a patch‑format diff that flags copies
git diff -p -C
```

Output you’ll see (excerpt):

```
diff --git a/old_file.txt b/new_file.txt
index abc1234..def5678 100644
--- a/old_file.txt
+++ b/new_file.txt
@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
 line1
-line2
+line2_modified
 line3
```

If `old_file.txt` actually exists elsewhere in the tree with the same content, you’ll get a line like:

```
 copy from :old_file.txt
```

or, when `--find-copies-harder` is used, a more detailed match may be reported.

### TL;DR

- **`-p`** → patch format  
- **`-C`** → detect copies (and renames)  

Combine them: `git diff -p -C` (add `--find-copies-harder` for a deeper copy search).

texts:
We need to answer: "What git reset options let me reset head but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command?" The user wants git reset options that reset HEAD but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command.

We need to provide the specific options: git reset --soft <commit> moves HEAD to commit, keeps index and working directory unchanged (so local changes stay). git reset --mixed (default) resets HEAD, resets index to match commit, but keeps working directory changes (as unstaged). But they want "skip refreshing the index after reset". That sounds like --soft maybe, or --hard? But they want keep local changes. Actually, "skip refreshing the index after reset" maybe means not updating the index (i.e., keep index as is). The option --soft does not touch the index nor working tree. --mixed resets index to match HEAD, but keeps working directory changes as unstaged. That does refresh the index though. The question: "reset head but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command?" Possibly they want `git reset --soft HEAD~1` which moves HEAD but keeps index and working tree unchanged, thus local changes preserved and index not refreshed. Or `git reset --keep <commit>`? There's also `--merge` option. Let's recall git reset options:

- `--soft`: does not reset index nor working tree, moves HEAD.
- `--mixed` (default): resets index to match HEAD, but keeps working tree files.
- `--hard`: resets index and working tree, discarding all changes.
- `--merge`: similar to --hard but safer when there are conflicts, used when aborting merge.
- `--keep`: resets index and updates working tree, but keeps changes to tracked files that are not moved; similar to --hard but more safe.

The user wants "reset head but keep local changes, and skip refreshing the index after reset, in the same command?" I'd answer: use `git reset --soft <commit>` to move HEAD while leaving index and working directory untouched, thus preserving local changes and not refreshing index. If they want to keep changes as unstaged, they could use `git reset --mixed <commit>` but that does refresh index. To skip refreshing index, use `--soft`. Provide explanation.

Thus answer: `git reset --soft HEAD~1` or `git reset --soft <target-commit>`. Also mention `--merge` maybe.

Will answer accordingly.</think>**Short answer**

```bash
git reset --soft <commit>
```

- **`--soft`** moves the `HEAD` (or any ref) to the named commit **without touching the staging area (index) or the working‑tree**.  
- Because the index and working directory are left exactly as they were, any local changes you’ve made stay intact and the index is **not refreshed/updated** by the command.

If you actually want the changes to remain in the working tree *as unstaged* files **and** you’re okay with the index being reset to match the new HEAD, you would use the default `--mixed`:

```bash
git reset --mixed <commit>      # same as `git reset <commit>`
```

But `--mixed` **does** refresh the index (it resets the index to the tree of the target commit).  

**`--hard`** would discard both the index and the working tree, so it’s not what you’re after when you want to keep local changes.

**`--merge`** and **`--keep`** are variants that also preserve working‑tree changes, but they are intended for special cases (aborting a merge, etc.) and they still update the index in some way.  

---

### Why `--soft` satisfies all three requirements

| Requirement                                 | What `--soft` does |
|---------------------------------------------|--------------------|
| **Reset HEAD**                              | Moves `HEAD` (or the ref you give) to the specified commit. |
| **Keep local changes**                      | Leaves the index and working directory untouched, so all your uncommitted edits, staged files, etc., remain exactly as they were. |
| **Skip refreshing the index**               | The index is *not* touched at all; it stays exactly as it was before the reset. |

### Typical usage

```bash
# Move HEAD back one commit, but keep all staged & unstaged changes
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Or target a specific commit/tag/branch
git reset --soft abc1234
```

After running this, `git status` will show the same changes you had before, and the index will still reflect whatever was staged before the reset. No “index refresh” occurs.
