---

## 1. Pull the `arm64` (aarch64) image of `ubuntu:24.04`

Docker lets you request a specific architecture with `--platform`.  
Running the command on your x86 host will pull the manifest for `arm64` and, if Docker can’t execute the image directly, it will automatically use QEMU to emulate the architecture (so you can run the container even though the host is x86).

```bash
# Pull the arm64 manifest; Docker will fetch the image and set up qemu‑user‑static if needed
docker pull --platform arm64 ubuntu:24.04
```

### What you’ll see

```
24.04: Pulling from library/ubuntu
...
Digest: sha256:xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Status: Downloaded newer image for ubuntu:24.04
```

Because we specified `--platform arm64`, the image’s manifest is stored as `arm64` even though the binary layers are accessed via QEMU on your x86 box.

### Running the container (optional)

```bash
docker run -it --platform arm64 ubuntu:24.04 /bin/bash
```

Inside the container you’ll see an `aarch64` kernel (the QEMU user‑space will translate system calls).

---

## 2. Suppress the progress bar in CI logs

When you run `docker pull` (or `docker build`) inside a CI job, the default UI shows a progress bar that can clutter the log output. Two common ways to turn it off:

| Method | Command / Setting | When to use |
|--------|-------------------|--------------|
| **CLI flag** | `docker pull --progress=plain` | One‑off pulls or builds in a script. |
| **Environment variable** | `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` (doesn’t hide the bar) – not useful for this case. | If you also want content‑trust signing. |
| **Docker daemon config** | Add `debug = false` or edit `daemon.json` with `"debug": false` – disables *all* UI, but also disables useful debugging output. | Rarely needed; usually over‑kill. |
| **CI‑specific** | In GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc., you can prefix the command with `DOCKER_CLI_EXPERIMENTAL=enabled` and then use `--progress=plain`. | When the CI runner already has Docker installed. |

### The most compact solution

```bash
# In a shell script or CI step
docker pull --platform arm64 --progress=plain ubuntu:24.04
```

`--progress=plain` replaces the interactive progress bar with a single line that only shows the pull status (e.g., `Pulling fs layer`), which is much easier to parse in log files.

#### Example GitHub Actions step

```yaml
steps:
  - name: Pull arm64 Ubuntu image
    run: |
      docker pull --platform arm64 --progress=plain ubuntu:24.04
```

The log will look like:

```
24.04: Pulling from library/ubuntu
Digest: sha256:...
Status: Downloaded newer image for ubuntu:24.04
```

No spinning bar, just the concise “Downloaded newer image” line.

---

## Quick cheat‑sheet

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| Pull arm64 Ubuntu 24.04 on x86 | `docker pull --platform arm64 ubuntu:24.04` |
| Pull with no progress bar | `docker pull --platform arm64 --progress=plain ubuntu:24.04` |
| Run the image (QEMU will translate) | `docker run -it --platform arm64 ubuntu:24.04 /bin/bash` |
| CI step (GitHub Actions, GitLab, etc.) | ```yaml\n  - run: docker pull --platform arm64 --progress=plain ubuntu:24.04\n``` |

---

### TL;DR

```bash
docker pull --platform arm64 --progress=plain ubuntu:24.04
```

That single line does exactly what you need: it fetches the `arm64` build of Ubuntu 24.04 for your Raspberry‑Pi testing and keeps the CI log clean by omitting the progress bar. Happy testing!

GIT-LOG(1)                                   Git Manual                                  GIT-LOG(1)

NAME
       git-log - Show commit logs

SYNOPSIS
       git log [<options>] [<revision-range>] [[--] <path>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Shows the commit logs.

       List commits that are reachable by following the parent links from the given commit(s), but
       exclude commits that are reachable from the one(s) given with a ^ in front of them. The
       output is given in reverse chronological order by default.

       You can think of this as a set operation. Commits reachable from any of the commits given on
       the command line form a set, and then commits reachable from any of the ones given with ^ in
       front are subtracted from that set. The remaining commits are what comes out in the
       command’s output. Various other options and paths parameters can be used to further limit
       the result.

       Thus, the following command:

           $ git log foo bar ^baz

       means "list all the commits which are reachable from foo or bar, but not from baz".

       A special notation "<commit1>..<commit2>" can be used as a short-hand for "^<commit1>
       <commit2>". For example, either of the following may be used interchangeably:

           $ git log origin..HEAD
           $ git log HEAD ^origin

       Another special notation is "<commit1>...<commit2>" which is useful for merges. The
       resulting set of commits is the symmetric difference between the two operands. The following
       two commands are equivalent:

           $ git log A B --not $(git merge-base --all A B)
           $ git log A...B

       The command takes options applicable to the git-rev-list(1) command to control what is shown
       and how, and options applicable to the git-diff(1) command to control how the changes each
       commit introduces are shown.

OPTIONS
       --follow
           Continue listing the history of a file beyond renames (works only for a single file).

                       `refs/remotes/` are not printed.

                       shown.

       identify the commit to other git commands.

           Instead of using only the annotated tags, use any ref found in refs/ namespace. This

           Instead of finding the tag that predates the commit, find the tag that comes after the

           Instead of using the default number of hexadecimal digits (which will vary according to

GIT-STATUS(1)                                Git Manual                               GIT-STATUS(1)

NAME
       git-status - Show the working tree status

SYNOPSIS
       git status [<options>] [--] [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Displays paths that have differences between the index file and the current HEAD commit,
       paths that have differences between the working tree and the index file, and paths in the
       working tree that are not tracked by Git (and are not ignored by gitignore(5)). The first
       are what you would commit by running git commit; the second and third are what you could
       commit by running git add before running git commit.

OPTIONS
       -s, --short
           Give the output in the short-format.

       -b, --branch
           Show the branch and tracking info even in short-format.

       --show-stash
           Show the number of entries currently stashed away.

       --porcelain[=<version>]
           Give the output in an easy-to-parse format for scripts. This is similar to the short
           output, but will remain stable across Git versions and regardless of user configuration.
           See below for details.

           The <version> parameter is used to specify the format version. This is optional and
           defaults to the original version v1 format.

       --long
           Give the output in the long-format. This is the default.

       -v, --verbose
           In addition to the names of files that have been changed, also show the textual changes
           that are staged to be committed (i.e., like the output of git diff --cached). If -v is
           specified twice, then also show the changes in the working tree that have not yet been
           staged (i.e., like the output of git diff).

       -u[<mode>], --untracked-files[=<mode>]

messages.content: A git reset --hard threw away a commit I needed. Recover it.

texts:
We need to help recover a commit that was thrown away by git reset --hard. We need to provide steps: using git reflog, git log, git reset, git cherry-pick, etc. Possibly also use git fsck. Provide instructions. No need to run commands unless user asks. So answer with guidance.</think>### Quick recovery plan – most of the time the commit is still in **Git’s reflog**

When you do `git reset --hard` the branch pointer moves, but the old commit objects are **not** deleted immediately – they stay in the local object store and are recorded in the reflog (a chronological log of every head change). If you act quickly (before any garbage collection runs) you can bring the commit back.

Below is a step‑by‑step recipe you can run in a terminal. Adjust the names (`my‑branch`, `main`, etc.) to match your situation.

---

## 1️⃣ Find the lost commit’s hash

### A. Look at the reflog of the branch you were on

```bash
# Show the last ~20 entries of the reflog for the current branch
git reflog
```

You’ll see something like:

```
abc1234 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving from abc1234 to HEAD~5   (reset --hard)
def5678 HEAD@{1}: commit: some feature I needed   (date)   <msg>
```

The entry just **before** the `reset --hard` line usually contains the commit you lost. Note the full 40‑character SHA (e.g., `def5678`).

### B. If you don’t remember which branch you were on

```bash
# Show the global reflog (all branches)
git reflog --all
```

or

```bash
# Show the reflog for a specific branch, e.g. main
git reflog main
```

### C. As a fallback, search with `git fsck`

```bash
git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs
```

Git will list every object that is no longer reachable from any ref. Look for a commit object (`commit <hash>`). The output will look like:

```
unreachable commit abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1
```

Copy that hash.

---

## 2️⃣ Bring the commit back

### A. Simple method – reset the branch to that hash

If you want the lost commit to become the tip of the branch you were on:

```bash
# Replace <hash> with the commit you recovered
git reset --hard <hash>
```

Now the branch points at the recovered commit and your working directory reflects its tree.

### B. If you want to keep the current branch tip and add the commit elsewhere

```bash
# Create a new branch at the lost commit
git checkout -b recovered-branch <hash>

# Or cherry‑pick it onto the current branch
git cherry-pick <hash>
```

`cherry‑pick` will produce a new commit with the same changes, leaving the original branch untouched.

### C. If you only need specific files/directories from that commit

```bash
# Extract a single file from the lost commit into the working tree
git show <hash>:path/to/file > recovered-file
```

---

## 3️⃣ Verify the commit is intact

```bash
git log --oneline <hash>
git show <hash>   # inspect the commit message, author, diff, etc.
```

If the commit contains sub‑modules or large files, make sure they are still present (git may have cleaned them up only after a GC, but that usually happens days later).

---

## 4️⃣ Prevent this from happening again (optional but helpful)

| Habit | How‑to |
|------|--------|
| **Keep a local backup branch** before big operations | `git checkout -b backup‑before‑reset main` |
| **Use `git stash`** for uncommitted work before resetting | `git stash` → `git reset --hard` → `git stash pop` |
| **Enable the “reflog expire” timeout** (rarely needed) | `git reflog expire --expire=now --all` |
| **Schedule periodic `git gc --prune=now`** only when you *intend* to free space | Not recommended as a safety net; keep reflog instead |

---

## 5️⃣ What if the commit has already been garbage‑collected?

Git’s **garbage collector** (`git gc`) removes unreachable objects after a grace period (default 2 weeks) or when you explicitly run `git gc --prune=now`. If that has happened:

1. **Check any remote you pushed to** – the commit may still be on another clone or on a fork.  
2. **Use `git fsck` with `--dangling`** on any other repository you have access to.  
3. **If you have a backup of the `.git` folder** (e.g., an archive), restore it and run the steps above.  
4. **As a last resort**, if you have a CI/CD pipeline or a backup service that archives Git objects, dig there.

---

### TL;DR (one‑liner)

```bash
# 1️⃣ Find the hash from the reflog
git reflog               # note the SHA just before the reset
# 2️⃣ Bring it back
git reset --hard <that‑sha>
```

If you follow the steps above you should see the commit re‑appear instantly. Good luck! 🚀

### 1️⃣ Unstage the file completely

```bash
# Unstage src/app.py (leaves the working‑tree file untouched)
git reset HEAD src/app.py

git restore --staged src/app.py
```

```bash
git add -p src/app.py
```

```
Stage this hunk [y,n,g,a/,e,d,?]?
```

| Key | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| `y` | Stage this hunk |
| `n` | Do **not** stage this hunk |
| `g` | Jump to the next hunk (skip) |
| `a` | Stage this hunk **and** all remaining hunks |
| `d` | Do **not** stage this hunk **and** skip the rest |
| `?` | Show help for other options |

```bash

# 1️⃣ Unstage everything
```

GIT-RESTORE(1)                               Git Manual                              GIT-RESTORE(1)

NAME
       git-restore - Restore working tree files

SYNOPSIS
       git restore [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] [--] <pathspec>...
       git restore [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] --pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]
       git restore (-p|--patch) [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] [--] [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Restore specified paths in the working tree with some contents from a restore source. If a
       path is tracked but does not exist in the restore source, it will be removed to match the
       source.

       The command can also be used to restore the content in the index with --staged, or restore
       both the working tree and the index with --staged --worktree.

       By default, if --staged is given, the contents are restored from HEAD, otherwise from the
       index. Use --source to restore from a different commit.

       See "Reset, restore and revert" in git(1) for the differences between the three commands.

OPTIONS
       -s <tree>, --source=<tree>
           Restore the working tree files with the content from the given tree. It is common to
           specify the source tree by naming a commit, branch or tag associated with it.

           If not specified, the contents are restored from HEAD if --staged is given, otherwise
           from the index.

           As a special case, you may use "<rev-A>...<rev-B>" as a shortcut for the merge base of
           <rev-A> and <rev-B> if there is exactly one merge base. You can leave out at most one of
           <rev-A>_ and <rev-B>, in which case it defaults to HEAD.

       -p, --patch
           Interactively select hunks in the difference between the restore source and the restore
           location. See the "Interactive Mode" section of git-add(1) to learn how to operate the
           --patch mode.

       -U<n>, --unified=<n>
           Generate diffs with <n> lines of context. Defaults to diff.context or 3 if the config
           option is unset.

       --inter-hunk-context=<n>
           Show the context between diff hunks, up to the specified <number> of lines, thereby
           fusing hunks that are close to each other. Defaults to diff.interHunkContext or 0 if the
           config option is unset.

       -W, --worktree, -S, --staged
           Specify the restore location. If neither option is specified, by default the working
           tree is restored. Specifying --staged will only restore the index. Specifying both
           restores both.

       -q, --quiet
           Quiet, suppress feedback messages. Implies --no-progress.

       --progress, --no-progress
           Progress status is reported on the standard error stream by default when it is attached
           to a terminal, unless --quiet is specified. This flag enables progress reporting even if
           not attached to a terminal, regardless of --quiet.

       --ours, --theirs
           When restoring files in the working tree from the index, use stage #2 (ours) or #3
           (theirs) for unmerged paths. This option cannot be used when checking out paths from a
           tree-ish (i.e. with the --source option).

texts:
The user wants to recover a commit that was thrown away by `git reset --hard`. Need to give instructions how to recover using `git reflog`, `git log`, etc. Provide steps. Also can check if any local repo? Probably just give general guidance.

We can also maybe check the reflog using bash, but we don't know the repo. We can give generic steps.

We'll respond.</think>**Recovering a commit lost after `git reset --hard`**

When a `git reset --hard` (or any other destructive operation) removes a branch reference, the commit objects themselves are usually still present in your local object store—they just aren’t reachable from any branch or tag. The easiest way to bring them back is to consult **Git’s reference log (reflog)**.

Below is a step‑by‑step recipe you can run in your repository.

---

### 1. Show the reflog

```bash
git reflog
```

You’ll see a list of recent actions, each entry looking something like:

```
abc1234 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving HEAD to abc1234
def5678 HEAD@{1}: commit: some message …   <-- this is where your commit lived
```

The `@{1}` (or `@{2}`, …) notation tells you the state *before* the most recent change. Locate the entry that corresponds to the commit you need—usually the one *before* the `reset` line.

### 2. Note the commit hash

Identify the full 40‑character SHA‑1 (or newer SHA‑256) hash of the commit you want to recover. In the example above it would be `def5678`.

### 3. Re‑create a reference to that commit

#### Option A – Move the current branch back to the commit

If you just want the commit to be on your current branch again:

```bash
git reset --hard <commit‑hash>
```

- This resets HEAD and the current branch to the saved commit, re‑creating any files that were in that tree.
- **Warning:** Any changes that happened *after* the reset will be lost, exactly as the original `reset --hard` did.

#### Option B – Create a new branch (recommended)

If you want to keep the recovered commit *and* preserve any work that was done after it, create a new branch pointing at that commit:

```bash
git checkout -b <new-branch-name> <commit‑hash>
```

Now `<new-branch-name>` points at the recovered commit, while your original branch stays where it is (usually at the point the reset moved it).

#### Option C – Cherry‑pick or merge

If you only need specific changes from that commit, you can cherry‑pick it onto any branch:

```bash
git cherry-pick <commit‑hash>
```

### 4. Verify the reflog entry is still there (optional)

Git’s reflog is kept for a default of **90 days** (configurable via `gc.reflogExpire`). After that period the entries may be purged. If you think some time has passed, you can still try:

```bash
git reflog --all
```

or look for dangling objects with:

```bash
git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs
```

If the commit object shows up, you can recover it with:

```bash
git checkout <commit‑hash>   # detach HEAD
# or
git branch -f <branch-name> <commit‑hash>   # force‑update a branch
```

### 5. Clean‑up (optional)

Once you’ve recovered the commit and are sure you have the work you need, you may want to expire the reflog early or run Git’s garbage collector to free space:

```bash
git reflog expire --expire=now --all
git gc --prune=now
```

---

## Quick “one‑liner” (if you already know the hash)

```bash
git checkout -b recovered-branch <commit-hash>
```

That creates a new branch `recovered-branch` pointing at the lost commit, leaving your original workflow untouched.

---

### TL;DR checklist

| Step | Command | What it does |
|------|---------|--------------|
| **1** | `git reflog` | Shows where HEAD has been; find the commit before the `reset --hard`. |
| **2** | Note the SHA from the reflog entry. | Gives you the exact commit hash. |
| **3a** | `git reset --hard <sha>` | Moves current branch back to that commit (discards later work). |
| **3b** | `git checkout -b <new-branch> <sha>` | Creates a new branch at that commit (safe). |
| **3c** | `git cherry-pick <sha>` | Applies the commit’s changes onto another branch. |
| **4** | `git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs` | Finds the commit if the reflog has expired. |

---

### What to do next?

- Run `git reflog` now and copy the hash of the commit you need.
- Then run one of the commands above (preferably the “create a new branch” option) to bring the commit back.

If you run into any trouble or want to double‑check the exact hash, feel free to share the output of `git reflog` and I can help you pinpoint the right commit.

messages.content:
GIT-STATUS(1)                                Git Manual                               GIT-STATUS(1)

NAME
       git-status - Show the working tree status

SYNOPSIS
       git status [<options>] [--] [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Displays paths that have differences between the index file and the current HEAD commit,
       paths that have differences between the working tree and the index file, and paths in the
       working tree that are not tracked by Git (and are not ignored by gitignore(5)). The first
       are what you would commit by running git commit; the second and third are what you could
       commit by running git add before running git commit.

OPTIONS
       -s, --short
           Give the output in the short-format.

       -b, --branch
           Show the branch and tracking info even in short-format.

       --show-stash
           Show the number of entries currently stashed away.

       --porcelain[=<version>]
           Give the output in an easy-to-parse format for scripts. This is similar to the short
           output, but will remain stable across Git versions and regardless of user configuration.
           See below for details.

           The <version> parameter is used to specify the format version. This is optional and
           defaults to the original version v1 format.

       --long
           Give the output in the long-format. This is the default.

       -v, --verbose
           In addition to the names of files that have been changed, also show the textual changes
           that are staged to be committed (i.e., like the output of git diff --cached). If -v is
           specified twice, then also show the changes in the working tree that have not yet been
           staged (i.e., like the output of git diff).

       -u[<mode>], --untracked-files[=<mode>]
           Show untracked files.

           The mode parameter is used to specify the handling of untracked files. It is optional:
           it defaults to all, and if specified, it must be stuck to the option (e.g.  -uno, but
           not -u no).

           The possible options are:

           no
               Show no untracked files.

           normal
               Show untracked files and directories.

           all
               Also show individual files in untracked directories.

           When -u option is not used, untracked files and directories are shown (i.e. the same as
           specifying normal), to help you avoid forgetting to add newly created files. Because it
           takes extra work to find untracked files in the filesystem, this mode may take some time
           in a large working tree. Consider enabling untracked cache and split index if supported
           (see git update-index --untracked-cache and git update-index --split-index), Otherwise
           you can use no to have git status return more quickly without showing untracked files.
           All usual spellings for Boolean value true are taken as normal and false as no.

           The default can be changed using the status.showUntrackedFiles configuration variable
           documented in git-config(1).

       --ignore-submodules[=<when>]
           Ignore changes to submodules when looking for changes.  <when> can be either none,
           untracked, dirty or all, which is the default.

           none
               will consider the submodule modified when it either contains untracked or modified
               files or its HEAD differs from the commit recorded in the superproject and can be
               used to override any settings of the ignore option in git-config(1) or
               gitmodules(5).

So they want a command that will move HEAD back one commit, but if there are uncommitted changes that would be overwritten, it should abort.

In git, `git reset --soft HEAD~1` moves HEAD back one commit but keeps changes in the staging area. `git reset --mixed HEAD~1` (default) moves HEAD back, resets staging but keeps working directory changes. `git reset --hard HEAD~1` discards everything.

Let's test: If you have uncommitted changes to a file that is also changed in the commit you are resetting to, git may refuse or modify. The safe way is `git reset --keep HEAD~1`. According to git docs: --keep: Resets files to the named commit, but keeps local changes that are not conflicting. If there are conflicts, it aborts. So that might be what they want: move back one commit, but fail (abort) if uncommitted changes would be overwritten.

Thus final answer.</think>If you want to move your branch back one commit **and** have Git abort (fail) rather than silently discard or overwrite any uncommitted work, use:

```bash
git reset --keep HEAD~1
```

### What it does
* Moves `HEAD` (and your current branch) back one commit (`HEAD~1`).
* Preserves any uncommitted changes in your working directory **as long as** they don’t conflict with the commit you’re resetting to.
* If the reset would overwrite uncommitted changes that conflict, Git **stops and returns an error**, leaving your branch and working tree exactly as they were.

### Quick comparison
| Option | Moves HEAD back | Keeps uncommitted changes? | Behaviour on conflict |
|--------|----------------|----------------------------|-----------------------|
| `git reset --hard HEAD~1` | Yes | **Discards** them | No warning – they’re lost |
| `git reset HEAD~1` (or `--mixed`) | Yes | Keeps them in the working tree (unstaged) | May silently change files |
| `git reset --keep HEAD~1` | Yes | Keeps them **only if safe** | **Aborts** with an error if unsafe |

So `git reset --keep HEAD~1` gives you the “move back one commit” behaviour while guaranteeing you won’t lose uncommitted work silently. If there’s any risk of data loss, Git will simply fail and your branch stays exactly where it was.

           included in the difference. All such pathspecs must be relative as they apply to both
           sides of the diff.

           This form is to view the changes you staged for the next commit relative to the named

           <commit> is not given, it shows all staged changes.  --staged is a synonym of --cached.

Pick the ones that fit your workflow; most people see a dramatic speed‑up just by disabling untracked‑file scanning and adding a few ignores.

---

## 1️⃣ Skip untracked‑file status (the biggest win)

Git has to stat every single file in the working tree when it decides “what’s new”.  
If you don’t need to see the list of untracked files, turn the feature off.

```bash
# Local repo setting – only affects this repo
git config --local status.showUntrackedFiles false
```

or, if you prefer a one‑off call:

```bash
git -c status.showUntrackedFiles=false status
```

*Result:* `git status` will instantly report only changes to **tracked** files.  
If you later want the untracked list, run `git config --local --unset status.showUntrackedFiles` or pass `--show-untracked`.

---

## 2️⃣ Ignore the stuff you don’t track

Even with untracked‑file scanning disabled, Git still has to read the `.gitignore` list to decide which files *would* be untracked.  
Make sure the biggest “noise” directories are excluded.

### a) Local `.gitignore` (only in this repo)

```bash
echo "node_modules/" >> .gitignore
echo "dist/" >> .gitignore
echo "*.log" >> .gitignore
# any build artefacts, caches, etc.
```

### b) Global excludes file (recommended for all repos)

```bash
# Create once, then point git at it
printf "node_modules/\n*.swp\n*.pyc\n.DS_Store\n" > ~/.gitignore_global
git config --local core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global
```

Now every repo you own will ignore those patterns without you having to edit each `.gitignore`.

---

## 3️⃣ Sparse checkout – only track the sub‑directories you actually edit

If the monorepo contains many independent packages, tell Git to care only about a whitelist of paths.  
After the initial set‑up, `git status` will only touch the selected trees.

```bash
# Enable the feature
git config --local core.sparseCheckout true

# Define the paths you want (add as many as you like)
git config --local core.sparseCheckoutPath src/pkg-a
git config --local core.sparseCheckoutPath packages/shared-utils
# …more paths…

# Populate only those directories (you can also use `git read-tree`)
git read-tree --prefix=src/pkg-a -u HEAD
git read-tree --prefix=packages/shared-utils -u HEAD
```

Now `git status` will instantly ignore everything outside those two directories.

*Tip:* If you frequently add/remove paths, you can toggle them with `git sparse-checkout set <path>` instead of editing config files manually.

---

## 4️⃣ Speed up submodule handling

Submodules can be a major source of slowness, especially when Git walks each one to compute its status.

| What to do | Command |
|------------|---------|
| **Disable recursive scanning** (only show the submodule’s current commit, not its whole tree) | `git config --local submodule.fetchJobs 0` (sets parallelism to 0, i.e. single‑threaded, but more importantly you can later use `--` to limit) |
| **Show only the commit** (instead of the full “modified” status) | `git submodule status` – much faster than `git status` when you have many submodules |
| **Avoid dirty‑check on every `status`** | `git config --local submodule.ignoreDirty true` – tells Git to treat a submodule as “up‑to‑date” unless you explicitly run `git submodule update` |
| **Shallow clone submodules** (only the latest commit) | `git submodule update --init --depth 1` |

If you never need to know whether a submodule’s working tree has dirty files, the simplest trick is:

```bash
git config --local status.submodulesummary false
```

(In newer Git ≥ 2.35 the default already omits the summary; if yours still prints it, turning it off saves a pass over each submodule.)

GIT-DIFF(1)                                  Git Manual                                 GIT-DIFF(1)

NAME
       git-diff - Show changes between commits, commit and working tree, etc

SYNOPSIS
       git diff [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [<commit>...] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <commit>...<commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <blob> <blob>
       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Show changes between the working tree and the index or a tree, changes between the index and
       a tree, changes between two trees, changes resulting from a merge, changes between two blob
       objects, or changes between two files on disk.

       git diff [<options>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you made relative to the index (staging area for the
           next commit). In other words, the differences are what you could tell Git to further add
           to the index but you still haven’t. You can stage these changes by using git-add(1).

       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]
           This form is to compare the given two paths on the filesystem. You can omit the
           --no-index option when running the command in a working tree controlled by Git and at
           least one of the paths points outside the working tree, or when running the command
           outside a working tree controlled by Git. This form implies --exit-code. If both paths
           point to directories, additional pathspecs may be provided. These will limit the files
           included in the difference. All such pathspecs must be relative as they apply to both
           sides of the diff.

       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you staged for the next commit relative to the named
           <commit>. Typically you would want comparison with the latest commit, so if you do not
           give <commit>, it defaults to HEAD. If HEAD does not exist (e.g. unborn branches) and
           <commit> is not given, it shows all staged changes.  --staged is a synonym of --cached.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --cached --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff --cached $(git
           merge-base A HEAD).

       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you have in your working tree relative to the named
           <commit>. You can use HEAD to compare it with the latest commit, or a branch name to
           compare with the tip of a different branch.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff $(git merge-base A HEAD).

           This is to view the changes between two arbitrary <commit>.

           If --merge-base is given, use the merge base of the two commits for the "before" side.

There's a git stash command that can include paths. Use `git stash push -p` or `git stash push config/` to stash changes in that path. The user wants to stash only changes under config/ and leave rest alone. So answer: run `git stash push config/` (or `git stash -- config/`). Also can use `git stash -p` to interactively select. Provide instructions. Might also need to keep other changes. So we can suggest: `git stash push -m "stash config changes" config/` . Also can use `git stash -- config/` (but older versions). Provide steps. No need to run bash unless they want to see current status. Could ask if they want to see status. But answer directly.

Thus final answer: command to run.</think>If you want to stash **only** the changes that live under the `config/` directory (while leaving everything else in the working tree untouched), you can use the `git stash push` command with a path limit.

### One‑liner

```bash
git stash push -m "stash config changes" config/
```

* `-m "stash config changes"` gives the stash a descriptive message (you can omit or change it).  
* `config/` tells Git to consider **only** the files inside that directory.

### What this does

| Action | Result |
|--------|--------|
| `git stash push config/` | Saves the current modifications, index changes, and untracked files **only** under `config/` into a new stash. |
| `git stash list` | You’ll see the new stash at the top; the original working‑tree files outside `config/` remain exactly as they were. |
| `git stash pop` (or `git stash apply`) | Re‑applies the stash later, again affecting only the `config/` files. |

### If you’re on an older Git version (< 2.23)

The `git stash push` syntax was introduced in Git 2.23. For older versions you can achieve the same thing with:

```bash
git stash -- config/
```

(That form stashes changes matching the path spec, but it’s less flexible than `git stash push` and won’t stash untracked files unless you also run `git add -u config/` first.)

### Quick checklist

1. **Commit or save any work you don’t want to lose** outside `config/` – the command only stashes what’s under that directory.  
2. Run the stash command above.  
3. Verify with `git stash list` and `git status`.  
4. When you’re ready, `git stash pop` will restore just those `config/` changes.

That’s it—your working tree outside `config/` stays exactly as it was, and only the `config/` modifications are tucked away in a stash.

GIT-RESTORE(1)                               Git Manual                              GIT-RESTORE(1)

NAME
       git-restore - Restore working tree files

SYNOPSIS
       git restore [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] [--] <pathspec>...
       git restore [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] --pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]
       git restore (-p|--patch) [<options>] [--source=<tree>] [--staged] [--worktree] [--] [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Restore specified paths in the working tree with some contents from a restore source. If a
       path is tracked but does not exist in the restore source, it will be removed to match the
       source.

       The command can also be used to restore the content in the index with --staged, or restore
       both the working tree and the index with --staged --worktree.

       By default, if --staged is given, the contents are restored from HEAD, otherwise from the
       index. Use --source to restore from a different commit.

       See "Reset, restore and revert" in git(1) for the differences between the three commands.

OPTIONS
       -s <tree>, --source=<tree>
           Restore the working tree files with the content from the given tree. It is common to
           specify the source tree by naming a commit, branch or tag associated with it.

           If not specified, the contents are restored from HEAD if --staged is given, otherwise
           from the index.

           As a special case, you may use "<rev-A>...<rev-B>" as a shortcut for the merge base of
           <rev-A> and <rev-B> if there is exactly one merge base. You can leave out at most one of
           <rev-A>_ and <rev-B>, in which case it defaults to HEAD.

       -p, --patch
           Interactively select hunks in the difference between the restore source and the restore
           location. See the "Interactive Mode" section of git-add(1) to learn how to operate the
           --patch mode.

       -U<n>, --unified=<n>
           Generate diffs with <n> lines of context. Defaults to diff.context or 3 if the config
           option is unset.

       --inter-hunk-context=<n>
           Show the context between diff hunks, up to the specified <number> of lines, thereby
           fusing hunks that are close to each other. Defaults to diff.interHunkContext or 0 if the
           config option is unset.

       -W, --worktree, -S, --staged
           Specify the restore location. If neither option is specified, by default the working
           tree is restored. Specifying --staged will only restore the index. Specifying both
           restores both.

       -q, --quiet
           Quiet, suppress feedback messages. Implies --no-progress.

       --progress, --no-progress
           Progress status is reported on the standard error stream by default when it is attached
           to a terminal, unless --quiet is specified. This flag enables progress reporting even if
           not attached to a terminal, regardless of --quiet.

       --ours, --theirs
           When restoring files in the working tree from the index, use stage #2 (ours) or #3
           (theirs) for unmerged paths. This option cannot be used when checking out paths from a
           tree-ish (i.e. with the --source option).

           Note that during git rebase and git pull --rebase, ours and theirs may appear swapped.
           See the explanation of the same options in git-checkout(1) for details.

       -m, --merge
           When restoring files on the working tree from the index, recreate the conflicted merge
           in the unmerged paths. This option cannot be used when checking out paths from a
           tree-ish (i.e. with the --source option).

       --conflict=<style>
           The same as --merge option above, but changes the way the conflicting hunks are
           presented, overriding the merge.conflictStyle configuration variable. Possible values
           are mer

GIT-DIFF(1)                                  Git Manual                                 GIT-DIFF(1)

NAME
       git-diff - Show changes between commits, commit and working tree, etc

SYNOPSIS
       git diff [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [<commit>...] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <commit>...<commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <blob> <blob>
       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Show changes between the working tree and the index or a tree, changes between the index and
       a tree, changes between two trees, changes resulting from a merge, changes between two blob
       objects, or changes between two files on disk.

       git diff [<options>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you made relative to the index (staging area for the
           next commit). In other words, the differences are what you could tell Git to further add
           to the index but you still haven’t. You can stage these changes by using git-add(1).

       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]
           This form is to compare the given two paths on the filesystem. You can omit the
           --no-index option when running the command in a working tree controlled by Git and at
           least one of the paths points outside the working tree, or when running the command
           outside a working tree controlled by Git. This form implies --exit-code. If both paths
           point to directories, additional pathspecs may be provided. These will limit the files
           included in the difference. All such pathspecs must be relative as they apply to both
           sides of the diff.

       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you staged for the next commit relative to the named
           <commit>. Typically you would want comparison with the latest commit, so if you do not
           give <commit>, it defaults to HEAD. If HEAD does not exist (e.g. unborn branches) and
           <commit> is not given, it shows all staged changes.  --staged is a synonym of --cached.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --cached --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff --cached $(git
           merge-base A HEAD).

       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you have in your working tree relative to the named
           <commit>. You can use HEAD to compare it with the latest commit, or a branch name to
           compare with the tip of a different branch.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff $(git merge-base A HEAD).

       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> <commit> [--] [<path>...]
           This is to view the changes between two arbitrary <commit>.

           If --merge-base is given, use the merge base of the two commits for the "before" side.

We'll respond with command and brief instructions.</think>**Command**

```bash
git reset --keep HEAD~1
```

**What it does**

* Moves the current branch back one commit (`HEAD~1`).
* If you have **any** uncommitted changes in the working tree or index that would be overwritten by that reset, the command **fails** and leaves your branch exactly where it was—your uncommitted work is preserved.
* If there are no conflicting uncommitted changes, the reset succeeds and your branch now points at the previous commit.

**Why this works**

`git reset --keep` is like `git reset --hard` for the files that *need* to change, but it refuses to discard local modifications that would be lost. When a conflict between the reset and your uncommitted work is detected, it aborts with an error message such as:

```
fatal: Unstaged changes would be lost by reset.
```

**Quick sanity check (optional)**

You can verify that you have uncommitted changes before running the command:

```bash
git status          # shows unstaged & staged changes
git diff HEAD       # shows unstaged changes
```

NAME

SYNOPSIS
       git describe [--all] [--tags] [--contains] [--abbrev=<n>] [<commit-ish>...]

       git describe <blob>

       The command finds the most recent tag that is reachable from a commit. If the tag points to
       the commit, then only the tag is shown. Otherwise, it suffixes the tag name with the number
       of additional commits on top of the tagged object and the abbreviated object name of the
       most recent commit. The result is a "human-readable" object name which can also be used to
       identify the commit to other git commands.

       By default (without --all or --tags) git describe only shows annotated tags. For more
       information about creating annotated tags see the -a and -s options to git-tag(1).

       If the given object refers to a blob, it will be described as <commit-ish>:<path>, such that
       the blob can be found at <path> in the <commit-ish>, which itself describes the first commit

           is appended to it. If a repository is corrupt and Git cannot determine if there is local
           modification, Git will error out, unless ‘--broken’ is given, which appends the suffix
           "-broken" instead.

NAME

SYNOPSIS
       git diff [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]

       a tree, changes between two trees, changes resulting from a merge, changes between two blob
       objects, or changes between two files on disk.

           next commit). In other words, the differences are what you could tell Git to further add

           included in the difference. All such pathspecs must be relative as they apply to both
           sides of the diff.

           give <commit>, it defaults to HEAD. If HEAD does not exist (e.g. unborn branches) and
           <commit> is not given, it shows all staged changes.  --staged is a synonym of --cached.

           If --merge-base is given, instead of using <commit>, use the merge base of <commit> and
           HEAD.  git diff --cached --merge-base A is equivalent to git diff --cached $(git
           merge-base A HEAD).

GIT-STATUS(1)                                Git Manual                               GIT-STATUS(1)

NAME
       git-status - Show the working tree status

SYNOPSIS
       git status [<options>] [--] [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Displays paths that have differences between the index file and the current HEAD commit,
       paths that have differences between the working tree and the index file, and paths in the
       working tree that are not tracked by Git (and are not ignored by gitignore(5)). The first
       are what you would commit by running git commit; the second and third are what you could
       commit by running git add before running git commit.

OPTIONS
       -s, --short
           Give the output in the short-format.

       -b, --branch
           Show the branch and tracking info even in short-format.

       --show-stash
           Show the number of entries currently stashed away.

       --porcelain[=<version>]
           Give the output in an easy-to-parse format for scripts. This is similar to the short
           output, but will remain stable across Git versions and regardless of user configuration.
           See below for details.

           The <version> parameter is used to specify the format version. This is optional and
           defaults to the original version v1 format.

       --long
           Give the output in the long-format. This is the default.

       -v, --verbose
           In addition to the names of files that have been changed, also show the textual changes
           that are staged to be committed (i.e., like the output of git diff --cached). If -v is
           specified twice, then also show the changes in the working tree that have not yet been
           staged (i.e., like the output of git diff).

       -u[<mode>], --untracked-files[=<mode>]
           Show untracked files.

           The mode parameter is used to specify the handling of untracked files. It is optional:
           it defaults to all, and if specified, it must be stuck to the option (e.g.  -uno, but
           not -u no).

           The possible options are:

           no
               Show no untracked files.

           normal
               Show untracked files and directories.

           all
               Also show individual files in untracked directories.

           When -u option is not used, untracked files and directories are shown (i.e. the same as
           specifying normal), to help you avoid forgetting to add newly created files. Because it
           takes extra work to find untracked files in the filesystem, this mode may take some time
           in a large working tree. Consider enabling untracked cache and split index if supported
           (see git update-index --untracked-cache and git update-index --split-index), Otherwise
           you can use no to have git status return more quickly without showing untracked files.
           All usual spellings for Boolean value true are taken as normal and false as no.

           The default can be changed using the status.showUntrackedFiles configuration variable
           documented in git-config(1).

       --ignore-submodules[=<when>]
           Ignore changes to submodules when looking for changes.  <when> can be either none,
           untracked, dirty or all, which is the default.

           none
               will consider the submodule modified when it either contains untracked or modified
               files or its HEAD differs from the commit recorded in the superproject and can be
               used to override any settings of the ignore option in git-config(1) or
               gitmodules(5).

           untracked
               submodules are not considered dirty when they only contain untracked content (but
               they are still scanned for modified content).

           dirty

GIT-STASH(1)                                 Git Manual                                GIT-STASH(1)

NAME
       git-stash - Stash the changes in a dirty working directory away

SYNOPSIS
       git stash list [<log-options>]
       git stash show [-u | --include-untracked | --only-untracked] [<diff-options>] [<stash>]
       git stash drop [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
       git stash pop [--index] [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
       git stash apply [--index] [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
       git stash branch <branchname> [<stash>]
       git stash [push [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-q | --quiet]
                    [-u | --include-untracked] [-a | --all] [(-m | --message) <message>]
                    [--pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]]
                    [--] [<pathspec>...]]
       git stash save [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-q | --quiet]
                  [-u | --include-untracked] [-a | --all] [<message>]
       git stash clear
       git stash create [<message>]
       git stash store [(-m | --message) <message>] [-q | --quiet] <commit>
       git stash export (--print | --to-ref <ref>) [<stash>...]
       git stash import <commit>

DESCRIPTION
       Use git stash when you want to record the current state of the working directory and the
       index, but want to go back to a clean working directory. The command saves your local
       modifications away and reverts the working directory to match the HEAD commit.

       The modifications stashed away by this command can be listed with git stash list, inspected
       with git stash show, and restored (potentially on top of a different commit) with git stash
       apply. Calling git stash without any arguments is equivalent to git stash push. A stash is
       by default listed as "WIP on <branchname> ...", but you can give a more descriptive message
       on the command line when you create one.

       The latest stash you created is stored in refs/stash; older stashes are found in the reflog
       of this reference and can be named using the usual reflog syntax (e.g. stash@{0} is the most
       recently created stash, stash@{1} is the one before it, stash@{2.hours.ago} is also
       possible). Stashes may also be referenced by specifying just the stash index (e.g. the
       integer <n> is equivalent to stash@{<n>}).

COMMANDS
       push [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-u | --include-untracked] [ -a
       | --all] [-q | --quiet] [(-m|--message) <message>] [--pathspec-from-file=<file>
       [--pathspec-file-nul]] [--] [<pathspec>...]
           Save your local modifications to a new stash entry and roll them back to HEAD (in the
           working tree and in the index). The <message> part is optional and gives the description
           along with the stashed state.

           For quickly making a snapshot, you can omit "push". In this mode, non-option arguments
           are not allowed to prevent a misspelled subcommand from making an unwanted stash entry.
           The two exceptions to this are stash -p which acts as alias for stash push -p and
           pathspec elements, which are allowed after a double hyphen -- for disambiguation.

       save [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-u | --include-untracked] [-a
       | --all] [-q | --quiet] [<message>]
           This option is deprecated in favour of git stash push. It differs from "stash push" in
           that it cannot take pathspec. Instead, all non-option arguments are concatenated to form
           the stash message.

       list [<log-options>]
           List the stash entries that you currently have. Each stash entry is listed with its name
           (e.g.  stash@{0} is the latest entry, stash@{1} is the one before, etc.), the name of
           the branch that was current when the entry was made, and a short description of the
           commit the entry was based on.

Thus final answer.</think>To stash **only** the changes that live under the `config/` directory (while leaving everything else in the working tree untouched) run:

```bash
git stash push -- config/
```

### What this does
* `git stash push` creates a new stash entry.
* The `--` (or you can just give the pathspec after the command) tells Git that the following argument is a **pathspec**, not a message or option.
* `config/` limits the stash to the tracked files that are under that directory.  
  * Only the modifications, staging area changes, and (if you also add `-u` or `-a`) untracked files inside `config/` are saved.
* The rest of your working directory—other modified files, other directories, untracked files, etc.—remains exactly as it was before the command ran.

### Optional flags
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `-u` or `--include-untracked` | Also stash untracked files under `config/`. |
| `-a` or `--all` | Stash **all** changes under `config/` **and** any other untracked files (equivalent to `‑u` plus staged changes). |
| `-k` or `--keep-index` | Keep the index (staging area) as‑is when popping the stash later. |
| `-m "message"` | Give the stash a custom description, e.g. `git stash push -m "config changes" -- config/`. |

### Quick checklist
1. **Commit / save any important work first** – stashing is temporary.
2. Run the command above.
3. When you’re ready to bring the stashed changes back, use `git stash pop` (or `git stash apply` if you want to keep the stash around).

That’s it—your working tree stays clean everywhere except for the `config/` changes, which are now safely stored in a stash.

I'll respond with suggestions.</think>Speed‑up `git status` in a massive monorepo usually boils down to a few config tweaks and a change in how you think about what Git should “watch”. Below are the most effective, low‑risk steps you can apply **per‑repo** (or globally) and the reasoning behind each.

---

## 1. Stop Git from listing untracked files

`git status` has to stat every file that isn’t already in the index. If you don’t need to see the exact untracked list, turn it off:

```bash
# In the repo (so it doesn’t affect other projects)
git config --local status.showUntrackedFiles no
```

*Result:* `git status` will still show the current branch, modified tracked files, and staged changes, but it will **not** enumerate the thousands of untracked files.  
*If you ever need the list*, run `git status -u` or `git status --untracked-files=all`.

---

## 2. Ignore submodule changes (or treat them as “clean”)

Submodules add a lot of overhead because Git has to look into each sub‑project’s working tree. Two options:

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **Never show submodule status** (fastest) | ```bash git config --local status.ignoreSubmodules all ``` |
| **Show only whether a submodule changed, not its internal status** | ```bash git config --local status.ignoreSubmodules dirty ``` |
| **Re‑enable later** | ```bash git config --local --unset status.ignoreSubmodules ``` |

If you have many submodules and rarely need their detailed state, the `all` setting cuts the “stat” work dramatically.

---

## 3. Skip the per‑file `stat` call (`core.ignoreStat`)

Git normally calls `stat(2)` on every file to decide if it changed. Setting `core.ignoreStat` makes Git rely on the index timestamp only, which is *much* faster on large trees (especially on network‑mounted repos or filesystems with slow `stat`).

```bash
git config --local core.ignoreStat true
```

*Trade‑off:* Git will no longer detect changes made **outside** of Git (e.g., editing a file with another editor and then committing). If you always edit through Git (`git add`/`git commit`), this is safe. If you sometimes edit files directly, you may need to `git reset` or `git update-index --refresh` occasionally.

---

## 4. Global/git‑wide ignore file

Put patterns that are *always* irrelevant (build artifacts, IDE files, generated code, etc.) in a global exclude file so every repo ignores them without you having to add them to each `.gitignore`.

```bash
# Create the file once (if it doesn’t exist)
touch ~/.gitignore_global

# Add typical monorepo noise
echo "node_modules/" >> ~/.gitignore_global
echo "*.md.bak" >> ~/.gitignore_global
echo "dist/" >> ~/.gitignore_global
echo "*.profraw" >> ~/.gitignore_global
# …add any other patterns you see repeatedly…

# Tell Git to use it
git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global
```

Now every `git status` (and `git add`) will skip those paths without you editing each repo’s `.gitignore`.

---

## 5. Sparse checkout / only track what you need

If the monorepo contains many directories you never touch, you can tell Git to **only** check out a subset:

```bash
# Enable sparse mode
git config --local core.sparseCheckout true

# List the directories you actually want (relative to repo root)
git config --local core.sparseCheckoutPath dir1
git config --local core.sparseCheckoutPath dir2/subdir

# Now only those directories appear; `git status` will be fast.
```

You can later add `git read-tree HEAD` after modifying the sparse‑checkout config to refresh the working tree.

*Use case:* when you routinely only work on a handful of packages/components.

---

## 6. Faster “what changed?” workflows

If you mainly need to see **which files** changed (not the full status), use more targeted commands:

```bash
# Recent commits only
git log --oneline -10

# Diff of the last commit
git diff HEAD~1

# Staged changes only
git diff --cached

# Unstaged changes (but still fast because it skips untracked)
git diff
```

These commands avoid the “untracked files” scan entirely.

---

## 7. Optional: Switch to a faster porcelain

Tools built on top of Git (e.g., **lazygit**, **tig**, **gitui**) can render status much quicker because they often:

* Cache the index.
* Show only the parts you ask for.
* Respect the `status.showUntrackedFiles` setting automatically.

If you spend a lot of time browsing the status screen, give one of these a try:

```bash

brew install lazygit   # macOS
apt-get install tig    # Debian/Ubuntu
```

“Pick hunk by hunk what to take back out of the index for `src/app.py`” is exactly the use‑case for Git’s **patch‑reset** (or **patch‑restore**) operation. It lets you interactively choose which hunks of a file you’d like to unstage (or revert) while leaving the rest of the file’s index entry intact.

---

## The easiest way: `git restore --patch`

```bash
git restore --patch src/app.py
```

or the short form

```bash
git restore -p src/app.py
```

When you run this Git opens an interactive selector that shows each hunk of the *difference between the current index and the working‑tree version* of `src/app.py`.  

- **`y`** – keep this hunk **unstaged** (i.e. take it out of the index)  
- **`n`** – keep this hunk **staged** (leave it in the index)  
- **`s`** – split the hunk into smaller pieces (useful for very large changes)  
- **`e`** – manually edit the hunk  
- **`q`** – quit without changing anything  

After you finish, the hunks you marked `y` are removed from the index, while the rest stay staged (or become unstaged if they were already staged).

---

## The equivalent older command: `git reset -p`

If you prefer the classic syntax (or your Git version doesn’t have `restore`), you can use:

```bash
git reset -p HEAD -- src/app.py
```

or the shorthand

```bash
git reset --patch HEAD -- src/app.py
```

The behaviour is the same: Git will present the hunks of the difference between `HEAD` and the current index for `src/app.py` and let you accept or reject each one.

---

## Quick checklist

| Goal                              | Command                              |
|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| **Unstage specific hunks only**   | `git restore -p src/app.py`          |
| **Unstage everything in the file**| `git restore src/app.py` (or `git reset HEAD -- src/app.py`) |
| **Use the older `reset -p` syntax**| `git reset -p HEAD -- src/app.py`   |
| **View what would be affected**   | `git diff --cached src/app.py` first |

---

```bash
$ git restore -p src/app.py
Select hunks to restore (and type their letters):
y - restore hunk to working tree
n - do not restore hunk
s - split hunk into smaller ones
e - manually edit hunk
q - quit
```

You’ll then be prompted for each hunk. Press `y` for the hunks you want **out of the index**, `n` for the ones you want to keep staged, and so on. When you’re done, Git updates the index accordingly and you can `git status` to verify.

---

- **`git restore -p src/app.py`** (or **`git reset -p HEAD -- src/app.py`**)  
- It opens an interactive hunk selector.  
- Choose `y` to take each hunk back out of the index, `n` to keep it staged.

       recently created stash, stash@{1} is the one before it, stash@{2.hours.ago} is also
       possible). Stashes may also be referenced by specifying just the stash index (e.g. the

There are two common ways to do this, depending on whether you want to keep the file staged and pick *which* hunks to keep, or start from a clean index and pick the hunks you want to stage.

---

## 1️⃣ Unstage unwanted hunks *in‑place* (recommended)

```bash
git restore --staged -p src/app.py
```

* `--staged` tells Git to work on the staging area only.  
* `-p` (patch) enters an interactive hunk‑selection interface.

### What you’ll see

```
Unstage this hunk [y]es/[n]o/[e]dit/[s]plit/[?] for more help?
```

You’ll be presented each hunk (a contiguous block of changes) one at a time.

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `y` | **Yes** – keep the hunk **staged** (do NOT unstage it). |
| `n` | **No** – unstage the hunk (remove it from the index). |
| `e` | **Edit** – let you manually modify the hunk before deciding. |
| `s` | **Split** – break the hunk into smaller pieces so you can choose individual lines. |
| `?` | Show help with all options. |

After you’ve gone through all hunks, Git will have removed only the ones you said “no” to, leaving the rest staged. You can then run `git commit` and only those hunks will be included.

---

## 2️⃣ Start fresh: unstage everything, then selectively stage

If you prefer to start from a clean index and add only the hunks you want, do:

```bash
# 1️⃣ Unstage the whole file (if it’s still fully staged)
git restore --staged src/app.py   # or: git reset HEAD src/app.py

# 2️⃣ Interactively pick which hunks to stage
git add -p src/app.py
```

### `git add -p` flow

You’ll see something like:

```
@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@
-def old_func():
+def new_func():
   pass
```

Again you’ll be prompted per hunk:

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `y` | Stage this hunk. |
| `n` | Do **not** stage this hunk. |
| `s` | Split the hunk into smaller pieces. |
| `e` | Manually edit the hunk. |
| `q` | Quit; remaining hunks will be left as‑is. |

When you’re done, `git status` will show only the selected hunks staged, ready for `git commit`.

---

## Quick cheat‑sheet

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| **Interactively unstage unwanted hunks** (keep the rest) | `git restore --staged -p src/app.py` |
| **Unstage everything, then add only wanted hunks** | `git restore --staged src/app.py` → `git add -p src/app.py` |
| **See what’s currently staged** | `git status` or `git diff --cached` |
| **Undo a mistaken unstash** | `git restore --staged src/app.py` (re‑stage the file) |

Let's provide solution.</think>**Short answer**

```bash
# Show the diff as text no‑matter how “binary” the file looks
git diff --text   # (or simply `git diff` with the right .gitattributes rule)
```

If you want this to happen automatically for every `.js` (or `.min.js`) file, add a tiny rule to **`.gitattributes`** in the root of the repository:

```
# .gitattributes
*.js diff=text
*.min.js diff=text
```

Then `git diff` will always treat those files as plain‑text and will emit the actual changes instead of the “Binary files differ” message.

---

## Why it happens

Git decides a file is *binary* when it contains a handful of non‑ASCII bytes or very long lines without line‑breaks. A minified bundle (`dist/app.min.js`) is exactly that kind of file, so Git falls back to its binary‑diff machinery and only reports “Binary files differ”.

## How to force text‑diff

### 1. One‑off: `--text` flag

```bash
git diff --text   # shows the real diff for any file, even binary ones
```

`--text` simply tells Git “pretend every file is a text file”, so it will generate a unified diff that you can scroll through, search, pipe to `patch`, etc.

### 2. Permanent: `.gitattributes`

Create (or edit) a file named **`.gitattributes`** at the top level of the repo and add:

```
# Treat all JavaScript files as text for diff purposes
*.js diff=text
*.min.js diff=text
```

Now every `git diff` (or `git show`, `git log -p`, &c.) will treat `*.js`/`.min.js` as plain text, regardless of how minified they are.

### 3. Regenerate the index (once)

After adding the attribute, make sure Git re‑evaluates the cached stat info:

```bash
git rm -r --cached .
git add -A
```

(Or simply run `git diff` again – the change takes effect for new diffs; the above just clears the cached “binary” flag for files already tracked.)

## What you’ll see

After either of the above, a typical diff will look like a normal unified diff:

```diff
--- a/dist/app.min.js
+++ b/dist/app.min.js
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-!function(e){t=n.r(e)}...
+!function(e){t=n.r(e)}...
```

The exact changed lines (even obfuscated ones) will be shown, allowing you to review what really changed between commits.

---

### Quick test (if you have a repo handy)

```bash
# Without --text (you’ll likely see "Binary files differ")
git diff dist/app.min.js

# With --text (you’ll see the actual lines)
git diff --text dist/app.min.js
```

Or, after adding the `.gitattributes` rule, just:

```bash
git diff dist/app.min.js
```

will already give you the diff.

---

### TL;DR

- **One‑command fix:** `git diff --text <file>`
- **Permanent fix:** add `*.js diff=text` (and `*.min.js diff=text`) to `.gitattributes` and `git rm -r --cached . && git add -A`.
- After that, `git diff` will emit the real changes instead of “Binary files differ”.

GIT-STASH(1)                                 Git Manual                                GIT-STASH(1)

NAME
       git-stash - Stash the changes in a dirty working directory away

SYNOPSIS
       git stash list [<log-options>]
       git stash show [-u | --include-untracked | --only-untracked] [<diff-options>] [<stash>]
       git stash drop [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
       git stash pop [--index] [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
       git stash apply [--index] [-q | --quiet] [<stash>]
       git stash branch <branchname> [<stash>]
       git stash [push [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-q | --quiet]
                    [-u | --include-untracked] [-a | --all] [(-m | --message) <message>]
                    [--pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]]
                    [--] [<pathspec>...]]
       git stash save [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-q | --quiet]
                  [-u | --include-untracked] [-a | --all] [<message>]
       git stash clear
       git stash create [<message>]
       git stash store [(-m | --message) <message>] [-q | --quiet] <commit>
       git stash export (--print | --to-ref <ref>) [<stash>...]
       git stash import <commit>

DESCRIPTION
       Use git stash when you want to record the current state of the working directory and the
       index, but want to go back to a clean working directory. The command saves your local
       modifications away and reverts the working directory to match the HEAD commit.

       The modifications stashed away by this command can be listed with git stash list, inspected
       with git stash show, and restored (potentially on top of a different commit) with git stash
       apply. Calling git stash without any arguments is equivalent to git stash push. A stash is
       by default listed as "WIP on <branchname> ...", but you can give a more descriptive message
       on the command line when you create one.

       The latest stash you created is stored in refs/stash; older stashes are found in the reflog
       of this reference and can be named using the usual reflog syntax (e.g. stash@{0} is the most
       recently created stash, stash@{1} is the one before it, stash@{2.hours.ago} is also
       possible). Stashes may also be referenced by specifying just the stash index (e.g. the
       integer <n> is equivalent to stash@{<n>}).

COMMANDS
       push [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-u | --include-untracked] [ -a
       | --all] [-q | --quiet] [(-m|--message) <message>] [--pathspec-from-file=<file>
       [--pathspec-file-nul]] [--] [<pathspec>...]
           Save your local modifications to a new stash entry and roll them back to HEAD (in the
           working tree and in the index). The <message> part is optional and gives the description
           along with the stashed state.

           For quickly making a snapshot, you can omit "push". In this mode, non-option arguments
           are not allowed to prevent a misspelled subcommand from making an unwanted stash entry.
           The two exceptions to this are stash -p which acts as alias for stash push -p and
           pathspec elements, which are allowed after a double hyphen -- for disambiguation.

       save [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-u | --include-untracked] [-a
       | --all] [-q | --quiet] [<message>]
           This option is deprecated in favour of git stash push. It differs from "stash push" in
           that it cannot take pathspec. Instead, all non-option arguments are concatenated to form
           the stash message.

           List the stash entries that you currently have. Each stash entry is listed with its name
           (e.g.  stash@{0} is the latest entry, stash@{1} is the one before, etc.), the name of
           the branch that was current when the entry was made, and a short description of the

**What it does**

Ok final answer.</think>Below are the few config tweaks and habits that turn a “git status ≈ 30 s” into “git status ≈ < 1 s” on a monorepo that has thousands of untracked files and several sub‑modules.

---

## 1️⃣ Stop scanning untracked files (the biggest time‑sink)

```bash
# Tell git: “don’t list untracked files unless the user explicitly asks”
git config --local status.showUntrackedFiles no
```

* After this, `git status` only reports changes to **tracked** files.  
* If you really need to see untracked files once in a while, run  
  `git status --untracked-files=all` or `git status -u`.

---

## 2️⃣ Make the “stat” check faster (stat → mtime + size)

```bash
git config --local core.ignoreStat true
```

* With `ignoreStat` = `true` git uses the file’s mtime + size instead of the full `stat` information.  
* This is a huge win when the filesystem is slow or when there are many files.

---


```text
*.tmp

build/
*.profraw
*.gcno
*.gcda
```

---

## 5️⃣ Use the porcelain / machine‑friendly output

```bash
git status --porcelain   # short, one‑line per file
```

* `--porcelain` omits the header “On branch …” and the long descriptions, so the shell can parse it instantly.

---

## 6️⃣ (Optional) Turn off colour & other UI overhead

```bash
git -c color.ui=never status
```

* A tiny speed gain on very large repos, especially when piping to `head`/`grep`.

---

## 7️⃣ Quick‑check cheat‑sheet

| Goal                              | One‑liner                                            |
|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Never show untracked files**    | `git config --local status.showUntrackedFiles no` |
| **Fast stat**                     | `git config --local core.ignoreStat true`          |

```bash
$ git status --porcelain
```

                    [-u | --include-untracked] [-a | --all] [(-m | --message) <message>]
                    [--pathspec-from-file=<file> [--pathspec-file-nul]]
                    [--] [<pathspec>...]]
       git stash save [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-q | --quiet]
                  [-u | --include-untracked] [-a | --all] [<message>]
       git stash clear
       git stash create [<message>]
       git stash store [(-m | --message) <message>] [-q | --quiet] <commit>
       git stash export (--print | --to-ref <ref>) [<stash>...]
       git stash import <commit>

DESCRIPTION
       Use git stash when you want to record the current state of the working directory and the
       index, but want to go back to a clean working directory. The command saves your local
       modifications away and reverts the working directory to match the HEAD commit.

       The modifications stashed away by this command can be listed with git stash list, inspected
       with git stash show, and restored (potentially on top of a different commit) with git stash
       apply. Calling git stash without any arguments is equivalent to git stash push. A stash is
       by default listed as "WIP on <branchname> ...", but you can give a more descriptive message
       on the command line when you create one.

       The latest stash you created is stored in refs/stash; older stashes are found in the reflog
       of this reference and can be named using the usual reflog syntax (e.g. stash@{0} is the most
       recently created stash, stash@{1} is the one before it, stash@{2.hours.ago} is also
       possible). Stashes may also be referenced by specifying just the stash index (e.g. the
       integer <n> is equivalent to stash@{<n>}).

COMMANDS
       push [-p | --patch] [-S | --staged] [-k | --[no-]keep-index] [-u | --include-untracked] [ -a
       | --all] [-q | --quiet] [(-m|--message) <message>] [--pathspec-from-file=<file>
       [--pathspec-file-nul]] [--] [<pathspec>...]
           Save your local modifications to a new stash entry and roll them back to HEAD (in the
           working tree and in the index). The <message> part is optional and gives the description
           along with the stashed state.

           For quickly making a snapshot, you can omit "push". In this mode, non-option arguments
           are not allowed to prevent a misspelled subcommand from making an unwanted stash entry.

GIT-DIFF(1)                                  Git Manual                                 GIT-DIFF(1)

NAME
       git-diff - Show changes between commits, commit and working tree, etc

SYNOPSIS
       git diff [<options>] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] [--merge-base] <commit> [<commit>...] <commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <commit>...<commit> [--] [<path>...]
       git diff [<options>] <blob> <blob>
       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]

DESCRIPTION
       Show changes between the working tree and the index or a tree, changes between the index and
       a tree, changes between two trees, changes resulting from a merge, changes between two blob
       objects, or changes between two files on disk.

       git diff [<options>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you made relative to the index (staging area for the
           next commit). In other words, the differences are what you could tell Git to further add
           to the index but you still haven’t. You can stage these changes by using git-add(1).

       git diff [<options>] --no-index [--] <path> <path> [<pathspec>...]
           This form is to compare the given two paths on the filesystem. You can omit the
           --no-index option when running the command in a working tree controlled by Git and at
           least one of the paths points outside the working tree, or when running the command
           outside a working tree controlled by Git. This form implies --exit-code. If both paths
           point to directories, additional pathspecs may be provided. These will limit the files
           included in the difference. All such pathspecs must be relative as they apply to both
           sides of the diff.

       git diff [<options>] --cached [--merge-base] [<commit>] [--] [<path>...]
           This form is to view the changes you staged for the next commit relative to the named
           <commit>. Typically you would want comparison with the latest commit, so if you do not
           give <commit>, it defaults to HEAD. If HEAD does not exist (e.g. unborn branches) and
